_comment: Health-review backlog — the parking lot for MINOR SYSTEM / PIPELINE / DOC issues a session noticed but did not fix (a stale comment, a small wiring gap, a doc that needs a touch, a flaky test). Per docs/CLAUDE-RULES-CANONICAL.md the session-end routine appends here instead of letting small issues rot. The autonomous /health-review skill drains this list every run: it triages each open item, fixes what it can, and marks it resolved. Do NOT use this for live-trading incidents or anything Tier-2/3 that needs immediate attention — raise those with the operator in chat. Three-way split (2026-05-26): STRATEGY / TRADING follow-ups go in docs/claude/performance-review-backlog.json; AI/ML EXPERIMENT follow-ups go in docs/claude/ml-review-backlog.json. Item ids here: BL-YYYYMMDD-NNN.

items.title: A stray trade_journal.db sits at the TRAINER's repo root holding 15,644 signals rows — the CWD-relative-fallback artifact canonical-db-resolver exists to prevent, and it nearly cost a false 'sync is 10 days stale' alarm
items.source:
MEASURED on the trainer VM 2026-08-12 via trainer-vm-diag #8817 and #8818. TWO journal DBs exist on that box:

  8,495,104 bytes   mtime 2026-08-02 04:50:22   /home/ubuntu/ict-trading-bot/trade_journal.db     <- STRAY (repo root)
  804,184,064 bytes mtime 2026-08-12 05:00:12   /home/ubuntu/ict-trading-bot/data/trade_journal.db <- the real one

Contents of the stray, read directly: `trades` 0 rows, `order_packages` 0 rows, **`signals` 15,644 rows**. Tables present: backtest_results, trades, strategy_versions, order_packages, signals, device_tokens, insights_history, insights_usage, balance_snapshots, learning_progress — i.e. a full schema, lazily created, with only the signals dual-write ever populating it.

STATE THE POPULATION: one filesystem read of one VM at one moment. I did NOT establish which process wrote it, and do not claim one — the mtime (2026-08-02) says only that nothing has written since, not what wrote before.
items.why_it_matters:
Two distinct harms.

(1) IT ALREADY CAUSED A FALSE ALARM, in this session. Querying the repo-root path returned `trades 0` and a 2026-08-02 mtime, and I reported the live->trainer DB sync as ten days stale before checking further. It is not: the real copy is 804 MB and fresh. A stray DB at the conventional path is a trap for exactly the read a session reaches for first, and the next session will reach for it the same way.

(2) It is the failure the `canonical-db-resolver` guard was built to prevent — the CWD-relative fallback that 'seeded the stray duplicate journals under each process's working directory' (CLAUDE.md, § Canonical persistence model). The guard forbids the pattern in tracked code, so either a writer predating the guard created this and it was never cleaned up, or something still resolves a repo-relative path on the trainer. Those need different fixes and I have not distinguished them.

The 15,644 stranded signals rows are a secondary matter: they are audit rows that never reached the canonical store, so any historical audit_query over that window on the trainer is short by an unknown amount.
items.resolution_criteria: Determine which process wrote the stray (grep the trainer's units + any cron for a bare `trade_journal.db` / a CWD-relative resolver, and check whether `signals` there has rows newer than 2026-08-02 on a later read — a growing count means a live writer, a frozen one means a historical artifact). THEN either fix the writer's path resolution, or, if it is confirmed historical, delete the stray and record that a later trainer-vm-diag `find / -name 'trade_journal*.db'` returns exactly ONE path. Deleting it before knowing which is the case would destroy the evidence of the writer.
items.next_action: One trainer-vm-diag read: re-stat the file and count signals rows to see whether it is still growing. Tier-1, read-only, and it decides between the two fixes.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: This is a file on the trainer VM, not in the repo — I cannot read it from this session. The repo-side guard that should have prevented it (canonical-db-resolver, forbidding the CWD-relative fallback) is in place per CLAUDE.md, so the stray is an artifact of a pre-guard writer or a shell path, and the remaining question is which writer still produces it. — needs live data: a trainer-vm-diag `ls -la /home/ubuntu/ict-trading-bot/trade_journal.db /home/ubuntu/ict-trading-bot/data/trade_journal.db` plus a row-count read of the stray's `signals` table, and `lsof`/`fuser` or a grep of the trainer's cron/service ExecStarts for a CWD-relative invocation. Ending condition: the writer is identified and routed through src.utils.paths.trade_journal_db_path(), and the stray is removed — leaving it invites the false 'sync is N days stale' alarm the row already nearly triggered.

Re-validated: same root as BL-20260814-TRAINER-CANONICAL-RESOLVER-POINTS-AT-EMPTY-JOURNAL — DATA_DIR unset on the trainer makes the canonical resolver return the repo-root stray. These two are ONE defect with two symptoms and should be worked together.

items.title: An instance of BL-20260730-PR-CI-NOT-ATTACHING was a MERGE CONFLICT, not a GitHub flake — mergeable_state is the first thing to check and the runbook does not say so
items.source:
OBSERVED on PR #8815, 2026-08-12 22:16-22:27 UTC. `pull_request_read get_check_runs` returned `total_count: 0` across three consecutive pushes (6135d05, an empty re-trigger commit 5e0a990, and the real commit 4bd3b68), sustained ~11 minutes. Runs existed for the three EARLIER shas on the same branch (5475a2d, ac8ed9e, 3aa3146) and none for the later three, so the workflow was not being created at all rather than created-and-unlinked.

CAUSE, read from `pull_request_read get`: `mergeable_state: dirty` and `base.sha` had moved 5a5ebdd -> 1a2922c (PR #8814 merged mid-session). GitHub does not run pull_request checks on an unmergeable PR. Merging origin/main and resolving one CLAUDE.md conflict restored checks IMMEDIATELY — 4 runs queued within seconds of the push.

What I tried first, and what it cost: an empty commit to re-fire the pull_request event (no effect, because the PR was still dirty), and a close/reopen cycle (no effect for the same reason, and it churns the subscription). Roughly 11 minutes and three pushes spent on workarounds for a condition one field would have named.
items.why_it_matters:
The existing row BL-20260730-PR-CI-NOT-ATTACHING describes the symptom (total_count 0) and prescribes workflow_dispatch as recovery. That prescription is WRONG for this cause and actively worse: guards.yml switches to `--all` on workflow_dispatch (line 124), so a dispatched run is whole-tree rather than PR-scoped and fails on pre-existing repo debt unrelated to the diff — producing a red that looks like the PR's fault. A session following the current runbook on a dirty PR gets a misleading red instead of a diagnosis.

The wider point is the one CLAUDE-RULES-CANONICAL already makes about zero-denominators: `total_count: 0` is a SYMPTOM with at least two causes (unmergeable PR / genuine Actions flake), and the runbook currently names only one. Treating them as the same thing is how the cheap diagnosis gets skipped.
resolution_criteria: TRIAGE RULE, documented where a session will hit it: a PR sitting at ZERO check runs must have `mergeable_state` checked FIRST (pull_request_read get). `dirty` = merge conflict, and GitHub does not attach checks to a conflicted PR. Only after that reads clean is BL-20260730-PR-CI-NOT-ATTACHING (genuine pull_request delivery drop) the right hypothesis. The two have the SAME symptom and DIFFERENT remedies -- resolve-the-conflict vs workflow_dispatch-by-hand -- so guessing wastes a dispatch round and can leave the real cause standing.

ROOT CAUSE OF THE RECURRENCE, which is what actually needs fixing: this repo SQUASH-merges. A long-lived session branch that keeps receiving commits after its PR is squash-merged can never match main, so the NEXT PR on that branch conflicts by construction -- it is guaranteed, not occasional. The cheap durable fix is the branch-restart already used elsewhere in this repo: after a squash merge, `git fetch origin main && git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-apply, INSTEAD of merging main back in.

Close when (a) the triage rule is written into the session-facing git/PR guidance so a future session spends 30 seconds not 30 minutes, and (b) the post-squash branch-restart is stated as the default in the same place.
items.next_action: Amend the existing row + docs/claude/ CI-recovery guidance. Tier-1 doc change.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: The resolution criterion is 'a later session finding that instruction present in the runbook it would actually reach for'. The mechanism IS recorded inside the antecedent backlog row (docs/claude/health-review-backlog.json, BL-20260730-PR-CI-NOT-ATTACHING, which now documents mergeable_state='dirty' -> no merge ref -> no run), but docs/claude/ci-status-checks.md — the runbook a session reaches for — contains no mention of mergeable_state, total_count, or checks-not-attaching (greps return nothing). The dangerous half is also unrecorded there: guards.yml switches to --all on workflow_dispatch, so the currently-prescribed recovery produces a whole-tree red unrelated to the diff.

RECURRED TWICE IN ONE SESSION, and the second time I misdiagnosed it.

PR #10171 sat at ZERO check runs across THREE pushes (9e82e49c, df72cdc1, eeff698d). Actions was healthy repo-wide -- scheduled workflows ran on main at 12:47Z and 12:50Z -- so 'CI is down' was already excluded by evidence, and I still reached for BL-20260730-PR-CI-NOT-ATTACHING (delivery drop) and hand-dispatched guards/pytest-run/pytest-collect via workflow_dispatch on that theory. The actual cause was `mergeable_state: "dirty"` -- THIS row. Resolving the conflict made checks attach within seconds, which is the confirmation.

WHAT MADE THE CONFLICT INEVITABLE: #10167 was squash-merged while the session continued on the same branch, so the branch carried pre-squash commits whose content main also had -- an add/add conflict on tests/test_protection_reassert.py plus a content conflict on this backlog file. The same shape had already cost a rebase earlier in the same session. This is not flakiness; it is what squash-merge + a long-lived branch does every time.

COST: roughly half an hour and a large number of tokens, on an issue the operator correctly called out as not worth that -- 'we can't just keep wasting tokens on this bullshit' -- with the explicit instruction that it be either fixed or backlogged properly rather than passed over. Hence the criteria above name the 30-second triage tell AND the durable fix, not just the incident.

NOTE ON THE BACKLOG MERGE ITSELF: resolving the conflict in this very file was done by diffing BY ID first (ours 830 rows vs theirs 829, ours a strict superset, the one differing row a pure append with theirs an exact prefix) before taking a side -- because BL-20260814-HAND-RESOLVED-BACKLOG-MERGE-SILENTLY-REVERTED-SIX-ITEMS-INCLUDING-A-RESOLUTION records what happens when that check is skipped.

RESOLVED. Operator reframed it correctly: 'the CI bug is really a workflow issue that we can resolve by explaining in the claude docs how to merge prs correctly.' Both criteria are now met in docs/CLAUDE-RULES-CANONICAL.md § 'Rule 3a — Branch mechanics around a merge' (binding, adjacent to the existing pre-merge compliance gate, which is where a session already looks before merging): (a) the triage table — zero check runs means read `mergeable_state` FIRST, with `dirty` and a genuine delivery drop called out as presenting IDENTICALLY and having opposite remedies; (b) the post-squash branch RESTART as the default, with the explicit note that merging main back in is what CREATES the conflict. Also carries the by-id backlog-merge rule and 'a missing check is not a passing check'. No code change — this was never a CI defect.

items.title: Provenance grades the SOURCE of a number, not whether it belongs to THIS row — so a duplicated netted pnl wore MEASURED and every provenance audit passed it
items.source:
MEASURED on the trainer journal 2026-08-12 (trainer-diag #8823, n=29 of 29 — the full marked population, not a sample). Every one of the 29 netted-duplicate rows carried `pre_remediation_exit_price_source = 'bybit_closed_pnl'`, which `provenance.classify_pnl` buckets as **MEASURED**, and `pnl_is_trustworthy` ADMITTED 29 of 29 before the remediation marking.

That is the opposite of the hoped-for result. The question asked was whether these rows were already excluded on other grounds; they were not. They were maximally trusted.

Why it is not a bug in `provenance.py`: `bybit_closed_pnl` is ACCURATE about the source. Bybit really did return that realized-pnl record. The defect is that ONE netted close's record was written to N sibling journal rows at full magnitude (`-2970.98599578` on 5 rows spanning 406x quantity, `659.29602983` on 3, `-767.21917054` on 3). Each row's `pnl` has genuine broker provenance and the wrong OWNER.
items.why_it_matters:
The provenance framework's whole promise is that a MEASURED grade means the number can be trusted for decisions. This is a class of wrongness it cannot express: MEASURED vs FABRICATED asks *where did this number come from*, and misattribution asks *does this number belong here* — an orthogonal axis with no field.

That orthogonality explains the months of silence. `docs/sprint-logs/S-PROVENANCE-EXITLEAK-ROOTCAUSE-2026-07-30.md` records that line-by-line audits kept returning clean because 'the defect lives at the seams'; this is the same shape one level up. Every provenance sweep over these rows returned MEASURED and was correct to. The duplication was found only when the P1.x R-axis normalised pnl by each trade's own risk and produced an impossible R (-99.5 on a 0.012 BTC position implying a ~$247,000 move) — i.e. by an ARITHMETIC impossibility, not by provenance.

The generalisation worth acting on: a per-row provenance grade cannot detect a defect whose evidence is CROSS-ROW. Duplicate detection is a set property. No amount of strengthening `classify_pnl` reaches it.
items.resolution_criteria: EITHER (a) a cross-row integrity check runs on a schedule and its result is readable on a diag surface — flagging any set of closed non-backtest rows sharing a pnl to 8 decimal places across quantities differing by more than a stated factor, reported with its denominator (clusters found / rows scanned) so a zero reads as a measured zero rather than a check that did not run; OR (b) a written decision in CLAUDE.md § 'Number provenance' records that provenance is explicitly scoped to source-not-attribution, naming misattribution as a separate axis and pointing at whatever does own it — so the next reader does not infer from a MEASURED grade that a value was checked for ownership. (a) is preferred; (b) is the minimum, because the current text invites exactly that inference.
items.next_action: The detection logic already exists as a one-off in scripts/ops/mark_netted_duplicate_pnl.py (the qty-spread + min-abs-pnl cluster selection). Promoting it from a manually-dispatched remediation action to a scheduled read-only check with a published denominator is the tractable version of (a). Tier-1.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Three concrete changes landed. (1) src/runtime/provenance.py:97-116 makes the scope explicit in the MEASURED docstring — 'this grades a value's SOURCE, not its OWNER … a per-row grade cannot detect it in principle: duplication is a property of a SET of rows' — cites the n=29-of-29 measurement and names this backlog id. (2) A dedicated FABRICATED source `netted_duplicate_unattributed` (:248) with the reasoning at :237-247, deliberately NOT spelled with the _prorated suffix. (3) The forward-side writer fix `_prorate_netted_broker_pnl` (src/runtime/order_monitor.py:4483, called at :4646 and :5594) plus the retroactive scripts/ops/mark_netted_duplicate_pnl.py and scripts/ops/repair_netted_misattributed_rows.py.

items.title: signal_audit.jsonl has grown to 501 MB on the live trader with no rotation timer, while its sibling shadow-prediction log HAS one
items.source:
MEASURED in system-action status-check #8813 (run 31644938442, timestamped 2026-08-12 21:58:50 UTC), section '--- runtime_logs alternative root (env-resolved) /data/bot-data/runtime_logs ---':

  /data/bot-data/runtime_logs/signal_audit.jsonl  size=501174992  mtime=2026-08-12 21:57:39

That is 501,174,992 bytes = 501 MB in ONE append-only JSONL. The same output reports vm_health disk at 40.8% of the 45 GB boot volume, so this is not yet an outage — it is a trend with no brake.

STATE THE POPULATION: n=1 sample, one moment (2026-08-12 21:58:50 UTC). This is a SIZE observation, NOT a growth RATE — I did not take a second point, so I cannot state MB/day and deliberately do not. Establishing the rate needs n=2 readings and is the first thing a fix requires; the 80% threshold named in the criteria below is therefore a target to project TO once a rate exists, not a projection I am making now.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, and it does not depend on the rate: `ict-shadow-log-rotate.timer` exists, is enabled+active in the same status-check enumeration, and rotates the shadow-prediction audit log daily. signal_audit.jsonl is the higher-volume of the two (a row per pipeline audit event across 52 strategies x 23 symbols per tick) and has no equivalent. One of two sibling append-only audit logs got a rotation timer and the other did not.
items.why_it_matters:
Three consequences, increasing in severity.

(1) DISK. The boot volume also holds /data/bot-data/trade_journal.db (the money DB). A volume that fills stops SQLite writes, which is a trading outage, not a logging one.

(2) READ SURFACES DEGRADE SILENTLY. /api/diag/audit and /api/diag/log_file?name=audit TAIL this file. CLAUDE.md already records they reach only the last _MAX_LIMIT=1000 lines, '~15 min of a busy day' — that window shrinks as the file grows denser, and nothing in the envelope announces it. That is the unasserted-denominator sub-class (C) of the diagnostic-provenance rule: a short tail reads like a quiet system.

(3) rsyslog.service showed 819.6 MB resident in the same cgtop output, the largest non-kernel consumer after page cache. Whether that is related is UNVERIFIED — I did not check whether rsyslog ingests this file, and assert no link.
items.resolution_criteria: Two points measured before any fix: signal_audit.jsonl size sampled twice at least 24h apart via status-check or /api/diag/log_file, yielding a stated MB/day growth rate over a named window. Then EITHER a rotation timer for signal_audit.jsonl is installed and observed to have rotated at least once (the file shrinks and a dated predecessor appears in the same directory listing on a later status-check), OR a written decision records why unbounded growth is acceptable, carrying the projected date the 45 GB volume reaches 80% at the measured rate. Also resolve whether rsyslog's 819.6 MB RSS is tied to this file, since that was left UNVERIFIED here.
items.next_action: Sample the size a second time (any status-check ~24h after 2026-08-12 21:58 UTC), compute the rate, then mirror the shadow-log-rotate unit. Tier-1 to measure; installing a timer on the live VM is Tier-2.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Confirmed asymmetric: deploy/ contains ict-shadow-log-rotate.{service,timer} rotating runtime_logs/shadow_predictions.jsonl (deploy/ict-shadow-log-rotate.service ExecStart runs scripts/ops/rotate_shadow_log.py --gzip), and there is NO equivalent unit for signal_audit.jsonl — greps of deploy/*.service and deploy/*.timer for signal_audit return nothing. The rotator is already generic: scripts/ops/rotate_shadow_log.py:167-178 takes a `--path` argument (default runtime_logs/shadow_predictions.jsonl). — Proposed change (Tier-2 — a new systemd timer the live VM consumes, so it needs one operator OK): add deploy/ict-signal-audit-rotate.{service,timer} as a copy of the shadow-log pair with `ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 scripts/ops/rotate_shadow_log.py --path runtime_logs/signal_audit.jsonl --gzip`, letting scripts/install_systemd_units.sh's auto-enable loop pick it up. Note the dependency to check FIRST: /api/bot/logs and /api/diag/audit tail this file and the trainer's setup_labels_audit dataset family reads it, so the rotation threshold must keep enough tail for both — verify what the rotator does with the active file before enabling. Current size 501 MB against a 45 GB boot volume at 40.8% used.

Re-validated and now COUPLED to a live constraint: the live VM reads 49.4% disk (fine), but the sibling trainer is at 91.7%. A 501 MB unrotated log while its sibling log HAS a rotation timer is an asymmetry with an obvious fix; ict-shadow-log-rotate.timer is active and is the model to copy.

items.title: Session env DIAG_BASE_URL still points at 158.178.210.252 — the x86 micro TERMINATED 2026-06-16 — so the documented 'try direct first' transport cannot succeed and costs a 10s timeout per session
items.source:
OBSERVED THIS SESSION at 2026-08-12 21:52 UTC. `env | grep DIAG` in the cloud session returned:

  DIAG_BASE_URL=http://158.178.210.252:8001
  DIAG_READ_TOKEN=<set>

CLAUDE.md section 'VM authority split' records 158.178.210.252 as the retired x86 micro, 'terminated 2026-06-16 via terminate-instance (by OCID, display_name ict-bot)'. The live trader has been 141.145.193.91 since the 2026-06-14 Ampere cutover — nearly two months.

VERIFIED the failure rather than inferred it: `DIAG_BASE_URL=http://141.145.193.91:8001 scripts/ops/diag_fetch.sh /api/diag/version` ALSO failed, curl exit 28 after 10s. So on this session's network level the direct transport is unavailable for either host and the issue relay is the only channel. The stale var is therefore NOT the sole blocker, and this row does not claim fixing it alone would restore direct access.
items.why_it_matters: docs/claude/diag-relay.md documents Transport A (direct) as PREFERRED with Transport B (relay) as fallback, and diag_fetch.sh's exit-3 contract routes between them. A var pointing at a terminated host means every session following the documented order pays a 10s timeout to learn nothing — and worse for trust, a session that reads the var without testing it could report the live trader's address as 158.178.210.252. The value is stale in a way that reads as authoritative.
items.resolution_criteria: EITHER the cloud environment's DIAG_BASE_URL is updated to the live trader (141.145.193.91:8001 or an HTTPS hostname for it) and a later session confirms `env | grep DIAG_BASE_URL` shows the new value; OR, if direct egress is intentionally unavailable at this network level, the var is UNSET in the environment and docs/claude/diag-relay.md is amended to state the relay is the only transport for sessions at Trusted network access, so sessions stop attempting a path that structurally cannot work. Either way a subsequent session must OBSERVE the changed state, not merely the doc edit.
items.next_action: Operator sets or clears the env var on the cloud environment (session env config is theirs, not settable from inside a session). Flagged rather than fixed for that reason.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Duplicate of BL-20260810-DIAG-BASE-URL-POINTS-AT-TERMINATED-MICRO and resolved by the same change. The stated harm — 'the documented try-direct-first transport cannot succeed and costs a 10s timeout per session' — is now false: scripts/ops/diag_fetch.sh:52-57 detects the retired 158.178.210.252 host, warns by name, and rewrites the URL to 141.145.193.91 before the curl at :65. I confirmed the env var is still the stale value in this session, so the self-heal path is the one that runs. — Residual is operator-only: updating DIAG_BASE_URL in the cloud-environment settings, which the script's own comment names as the permanent fix.

items.title: status_check.sh's collapsed-state fix was code-verified but its NEGATIVE branch had never been exercised — the live verification only proved the happy path
items.source:
status-check #8813 (run 31644938442, 2026-08-12 21:58:50 UTC), dispatched to verify the two fixes in 5a5ebdd for BL-20260811-STATUSCHECK-PID-LOOKUP-AND-STALE-REPO-HEARTBEAT. VM confirmed at git_sha 5a5ebdde via /api/diag/version, so the fixed code was live.

VERIFIED LIVE, 2 of 3: the env dump now runs for a RUNNING trader ('trader pid: 939707' + 'DATA_DIR=/data/bot-data' where it previously printed the not-found string, cross-checked against the same report's ps showing PID 939707 at 21.2% CPU, 7329s elapsed); and the repo-path block now carries the LEGACY label so its 2026-06-14 mtime cannot be misread as the answer.

NOT VERIFIED at filing: the 'WE COULD NOT LOOK' branch. /proc/939707/environ was readable on that run, so the unreadable-environ path did not execute — and that branch carries the entire point of a collapsed-state fix.
items.why_it_matters: The parent row's whole subject was a COLLAPSED STATE: 'we could not look' being indistinguishable from 'it is not there'. Verifying the happy path of a collapsed-state fix confirms the least interesting half.
items.resolution_criteria: A test exercises the unreadable-/proc path and asserts the output contains a distinct could-not-look string that is NOT the process-absent string — the two must be different literals, asserted as different, so a later refactor collapsing them fails. Passing under the repo's normal pytest run is sufficient; a live unreadable-environ occurrence is not required.
items.resolution: RESOLVED same session by tests/test_status_check_pid_three_states.py (5 tests). The test EXTRACTS the if/elif/else block from the shipped scripts/ops/status_check.sh text rather than copying it, so a collapse fails there regardless of what a copy would have said, and asserts the three messages are pairwise distinct after normalising the PID out. Verified against a planted defect: restoring the ACTUAL pre-fix string '(trader pid not found or /proc unreadable — env dump skipped)' into both branches fails 3 of 5, including the distinctness assertion, which prints the two identical strings side by side.

items.title: Wall-clock time-bomb tests (fixed date literal vs a now()-relative window) have no sound detector — one instance reddened main on 2026-08-12 and a 234-file sweep found no second, but the sweep instrument produces FALSE POSITIVES and cannot be trusted as a clean bill of health
items.source:
Found 2026-08-12 when `tests/test_exchange_fills_list_rows.py::test_newest_first` failed on clean origin/main, blocking every open PR. Mechanism: fixed August-2026 fixture literals measured against a window computed from `datetime.now()`, so a test about ORDERING silently depended on the date it ran on. Fixed in PR #8778 by injecting a fixed clock BY DEFAULT (a `_list()` helper) rather than patching the one call site that broke; verified clock-independent at +/-400d and still able to fail on planted defects (reversed ORDER BY, ignored window).

MEASURED BLAST RADIUS OF THAT ONE INSTANCE, before the fix: with the module clock advanced against clean main, 1 test failed on 2026-08-12 and 7 of the 13 in that file failed from 2026-08-13 onward (because `_fill` defaults to 2026-08-06). Fixing only the day's red one would have re-reddened main the next day.
items.why_it_matters: This class fails CLOSED on a date nobody chose, on main, for every open PR at once, and presents identically to a real defect: the failing assertion is about ordering/filters/truncation, not about time, so the reader hunts the wrong thing. It is also self-inflicted and cheap to prevent — the sibling test in the same file already injected `now` for exactly this reason and its docstring argues the point, so the lesson existed in one test and had never reached its neighbours.
items.what_to_check: A SOUND detector for: a test carrying a hardcoded date literal that is compared against a window derived from `datetime.now()` (directly or through a function whose default is now-relative). The two candidate approaches: (a) a static check — flag a test file with a `"20NN-NN-NN"` literal that calls a windowing API without passing `now=`; (b) a real clock-freezing run — needs `freezegun` or `time-machine`, NEITHER of which is installed in this repo today.
items.action: LOW priority, and deliberately not urgent — the only known instance is fixed and the sweep found no second. If picked up: prefer the STATIC check (a), since it detects the pattern rather than its symptom and needs no new dependency. Do NOT rebuild the dynamic clock-shift sweep described below without fixing its two defects first.
items.sweep_result_and_why_the_instrument_is_n:
SWEEP RUN 2026-08-12 over the 234 test files containing 2025/2026 date literals (3,554 tests, 0 failures at +0d). RESULT: no second instance of the genuine class. But the instrument is NOT sound and its output must not be read as a clean bill of health.

DEFECT 1 - FALSE POSITIVES FROM CLOCK SKEW. The first version patched `datetime` only on `src.*`/`scripts.*`/`ml.*` module bindings. A test that builds its fixture from `datetime.now()` IN THE TEST MODULE then saw real time while the code under test saw now+Nd, so any bounded window failed spuriously: `test_readopt_guard_suppresses_flapping_position` inserts a row closed `now-10s` and asserts a 300s re-adopt guard suppresses it — a 1-DAY skew defeats a 300-SECOND window. That reported 20 non-bombs as bombs at +1d. Patching test modules too dropped it to 7.

DEFECT 2 - FUNCTION-LOCAL IMPORTS ARE UNREACHABLE. All 7 survivors are ALSO now()-relative: e.g. `tests/test_pairs_executor.py::test_reconstruct_open_state_from_pkg_meta` does `from datetime import datetime` INSIDE the function body, rebinding the real class after any module-level patch. So the residual 7 are the same skew artifact one level deeper, not findings.

THE ASYMMETRY WORTH RECORDING. Four instrument bugs occurred in this one sweep. Three produced false NEGATIVES and failed safe (a 15-min `timeout` that truncated the run and emitted no summary line; a file list built with `grep -rl` that matched `__pycache__/*.pyc` and made pytest exit 4; an output file read while the second arm was still running). The FOURTH produced a confident false POSITIVE — 20 named tests, a plausible severity, and an alarming 'main breaks tomorrow' story that would have sent another session hunting 20 non-bugs and taught the board to discount the next real alarm. A detector that over-reports costs trust in the alarm itself, which is the desensitised-alarm P1 shape approached from the opposite side. Any rebuild must carry a POSITIVE CONTROL (this one did: it reproduced the known 7 pre-fix failures at +1d on clean main, which is the only reason its later output was checked at all rather than believed).
items.resolution_criteria: Either (a) a static guard that flags a hardcoded-literal-vs-now-window test and is proven on the pre-fix `test_newest_first` as a positive control, or (b) a documented decision that the class is rare enough to handle reactively — recorded WITH the sweep's method limitations above, so the next session does not re-derive the same broken dynamic detector and act on its false positives.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Neither candidate approach shipped. There is no timebomb/wallclock detector under scripts/ or scripts/ci/, and neither freezegun nor time-machine appears in requirements.txt / requirements-dev.txt / requirements-test.txt — so the clock-freezing option is still unavailable in this repo. — Legitimately deferred: the row itself records that the one known instance was fixed (PR #8778, fixed clock injected by default) and that a 234-file sweep found no second, but with an instrument that produces false positives — so a clean bill of health is not available either. Ending condition: either a sound static check (a test file with a '20NN-NN-NN' literal calling a now-relative windowing API without passing now=) with a planted positive control, or a recorded decision that the class is rare enough to accept.
Re-validated: a test that reddens main on a date rollover has no sound detector. Cheap CI-side fix; still undone.

items.title: The M20 sweep corpus records every CONFIG axis of a measurement (split, tp_cap, fee, regime book, trades floor, confidence floor) but NOT the DATA it ran on — structural gap, NO observed instance: the 0.20 arm reproduced the 15bps control on 3 of 3 legs across a 50-minute frame-refetch gap
items.source:
Filed and corrected 2026-08-12 while running the SRQ-20260618-003 confidence arms on PR #8778 (control run 31544988689 at ~23:04Z; arms 31548326840/31548334325/31548340442 at ~23:56Z).

POPULATION for the replication claim: 3 legs (ict_scalp_{eth,sol,xrp}_15m), all 3 reproduced the control exactly at min_confidence=0.20 — a floor that is provably inert for this family (config/strategies.yaml::ict_scalp_5m sets min_displacement_body_to_range 0.55, enforced as an ENTRY REJECTION at src/units/strategies/ict_scalp.py:222, and confidence at :537 is 0.4*body_to_range + two non-negative terms, so every admitted setup scores >= 0.4*0.55 = 0.22 > 0.20; the harness reads that same value at scripts/backtest_ict_scalp.py:487). So the arm doubled as an unplanned determinism check and passed on 3 of 3.
items.why_it_matters: The corpus measurement_key was extended four times this week — tp_cap_pct, regime_router, min_oos_trades_floor, fee_bps_roundtrip — each on the argument that two runs differing on that axis measured DIFFERENT BOOKS and must not merge under one label. The frames are the same kind of axis and the one nobody records: a row asserts what was CONFIGURED and is silent on what was MEASURED. That remains true. What is NOT true, and what this item originally claimed, is that it has bitten.
items.action: LOW priority, and deliberately not urgent. If picked up: stamp a per-leg frame fingerprint (row count + first/last bar timestamp + a content hash, all three so a truncated frame and a shifted one stay distinguishable) into verdicts.json and propagate it to the corpus row the way fee_bps_roundtrip is. RECORD but do NOT add it to measurement_key — keying on it would stop a re-run ever superseding an older row, which is the opposite of what the merge exists for; the right analogue is regime_gate_delta, recorded and deliberately excluded from the key. A reported mismatch when two rows share a key and differ on frames is the useful half.
items.correction_2026_08_12:
CORRECTED 2026-08-12T00:35Z, SAME SESSION, BEFORE THIS ITEM WAS EVER READ BY ANYONE ELSE. As first filed, this item's central claim was FALSE and I am recording that rather than editing the numbers quietly.

WHAT I FILED: that ict_scalp_sol_15m moved OOS 142 -> 141 between the 15bps control and the min_confidence=0.20 arm with 'no config difference that could cause it', and that the delta was therefore data-side drift.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY TRUE: the 141 reading belongs to the **0.30** arm, not the 0.20 arm. I attributed a PR sweep comment to the wrong run. The corpus — which does key on min_confidence_override — says plainly: at 0.20 sol is 280/142 and at 0.30 it is 280/141. The 0.30 floor skipped one sol entry; that is a CONFIG difference, fully explaining the delta.

THE EVIDENCE INVERTS. The 0.20 arm reproduced the control on ALL THREE legs — eth 257/130, sol 280/142, xrp 227/134 — with byte-identical cell tables, across frames re-fetched from the trainer ~50 minutes after the control's. That is a clean replication, i.e. positive evidence that the frames were STABLE over that window, which is the opposite of the drift I filed.

ROOT CAUSE OF MY ERROR, and it is the point worth keeping: the PR sweep comment did not name the arm. Three near-identical comments were in flight and the only distinguishing field was a trade count I had to guess from. I had ALREADY identified that gap and fixed the banner (commit 21032b5, fee + confidence floor now printed) — and then fell into it anyway on the runs that predated the fix. An identity field that is missing does not just cost a reader time; it actively produced a confident wrong finding from correct raw data.

DISPOSITION: severity medium -> LOW and the claim rescoped to what it is — a STRUCTURAL gap with no observed instance. It is still real (a re-run months from now genuinely would read different frames, and nothing in a corpus row would say so), but it is not urgent and it is explicitly NOT supported by tonight's data. Do not cite this item as evidence that drift has been seen.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Confirmed on disk: scripts/research/m20_fleet_exit_sweep.py records the config axes into the corpus (:2277-2287 — split, split_target_oos, tp_cap_pct, fee_bps_roundtrip, regime_router, min_oos_trades_floor) and greps for frame_fingerprint / data_md5 / data_sha / frame_rows / data_first_ts return nothing. The gap is exactly as filed: structural, with no observed instance. — Duplicate substrate with BL-20260810-SWEEP-VERDICTS-DO-NOT-RECORD-THEIR-DATASET — one change closes both, and that row DOES have an observed near-instance (two different ETHUSDT_15m files in active use with different md5s and different usable-fold counts), which is the better justification.

resolution_criteria AUTHORED. This row was one of 70 open rows that could never be retired because nothing said what would retire it (BL-20260825-KEPT-OPEN-ROWS-WITH-NO-EXIT-CONDITION-CAN-NEVER-BE-RETIRED). The criterion is derived from THIS row's own recorded material, not from a template - 53 of the 70 carry no material and are deliberately left for genuine authorship rather than given a generic exit condition, which would be the same defect wearing a criteria field.

Re-validated: a measurement that records every CONFIG axis but not the DATA it ran on cannot be reproduced or invalidated later. Same family as BL-20260813-HARNESS-SYMBOL-IS-A-LABEL-DATA-DEFAULTS-TO-BTC.

items.resolution_criteria: Either (a) verdicts.json carries a per-leg frame fingerprint - row count AND first/last bar timestamp AND a content hash, all three, so a truncated frame and a shifted one stay distinguishable - propagated to the corpus row the way fee_bps_roundtrip is, RECORDED and deliberately ABSENT from measurement_key, with a mismatch reported when two rows share a key and differ on frames; or (b) a recorded decision that the structural gap is accepted, naming the observation that would reopen it. Adding the fingerprint TO measurement_key does not satisfy this - the row states why (it would stop a re-run ever superseding an older row).

items.title: /api/diag/shadow_stats served the UNDISCLOSED first_seen — the soak-basis disclosure and registry recovery (#8774) landed only on /api/bot/shadow/stats, which a relay-bound session cannot reach
items.source:
Found 2026-08-12 while trying to VERIFY #8774 end-to-end (diag #8800). The diag mirror built its own row dicts (model_id/stage/count/score_*/first_seen/last_seen) and never gained the fields #8774 added to the public handler: `soak_start_basis`, `soak_started_at`, `soak_days`, `soak_days_is_lower_bound`, plus the `log_coverage` and `registry_soak_source` envelope blocks.
MEASURED on the live fleet in the same read: all 30 models reported `first_seen` inside a ~2-minute band (2026-08-05T23:35-23:37) on a 20.6 MB log — a rotation boundary, not 30 simultaneous soak starts. BOTH advisory heads were promoted BEFORE that boundary (sol-regime-15m-lgbm-fc-pcv-v2 2026-08-02, btc-regime-15m-lgbm-fc-pcv-v2 2026-08-04), so their soak read ~6.0 days against a genuinely longer one. That is exactly the `log_censored` case #8774 built the recovery for, and it was invisible here.
items.what_to_check: src/web/api/routers/diag.py::get_shadow_stats vs src/web/api/routers/shadow.py::stats. The divergence is the general risk, not this one field: any future enrichment of the public handler would have skipped the mirror the same way.
items.why_critical: The mirror's stated purpose (per its own docstring, added 2026-05-16) is 'so Layer-2 health reviews can audit WITHOUT SSH' — so it is the ONLY shadow-stats surface a PM-side/relay-bound session can reach, and the health/ml review skills judge promotion readiness from exactly that surface. #8774's whole point was that `first_seen` is a LOWER BOUND after rotation and must never be read bare, because the error makes a long soak look short and a promotion that is DUE reads as not-yet-ready. Shipping the disclosure only where the relay cannot see it left the fix reachable everywhere except where it was needed — the same written-but-not-readable shape as the exposure block that had no reader (#8665).
items.next_action: RESOLVED 2026-08-12: the diag route now DELEGATES to the public handler rather than re-deriving rows, so there is ONE definition of a soak start instead of two free to drift. Verified against a synthetic rotated log: the delegated response returns soak_start_basis='log_censored' with soak_days_is_lower_bound set, plus the log_coverage + registry_soak_source envelope blocks. Log-path resolution was confirmed byte-equivalent between the two before delegating, so this changes no file being read. Re-confirm on the live fleet after merge + git-sync via a fresh `shadow_stats` diag.
items.resolution_criteria: A relay `shadow_stats` read that carries soak_start_basis per row and the registry_soak_source envelope — i.e. a relay-bound session can tell a censored lower-bound soak from a real one without SSH.

items.title: GitHub Actions runners intermittently fail git over TLS ('server certificate verification failed'), and the job reports conclusion=failure indistinguishable from a real test/guard failure
items.source:
Observed THREE times in ~70 minutes on 2026-08-11/12, across two different workflows and two different steps, on PR #8796:
  (a) guards run 31545035369 attempt 1 (sha f4cae14) -- actions/checkout could not clone; three retries (19s/10s/final), all TLS-failed, job over in ~30s.
  (b) pytest-collect run 31548473662 (sha 3002a33) -- failed in the CHANGED-FILES step's `git diff` against the base ref, i.e. AFTER checkout succeeded.
Error is identical in both: `fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/benbaichmankass/Metis-Insights/': server certificate verification failed. CAfile: none CRLfile: none`.
Both cleared on `rerun_failed_jobs` against the IDENTICAL sha, which is what establishes them as infra rather than content.
items.what_to_check: Whether this is a GitHub-side incident (check githubstatus.com history for 2026-08-11 ~22:40-00:00Z) or something about this repo's runner image. Note Actions was ALSO degraded on latency that night -- guards normally completes in ~30s and both attempts on run 31545035369 ran 5+ minutes -- so the TLS failures may be one symptom of a broader incident rather than a standing defect.
items.why_critical: Not critical to trading -- nothing trades on CI. It matters because of HOW it presents: the webhook and the check-run API both report `conclusion: failure` with the check name (`guards`, `pytest-collect`), which is byte-identical to a real guard/test failure. A session reacting to the notification without opening the log will hunt for a defect in its own diff that does not exist, and -- worse -- a session that has learned to expect this may start waving off REAL reds as 'probably the TLS thing'. That second failure mode is the desensitized-alarm P1 shape the repo's 'if you see something, say something' rule names explicitly.
items.next_action: No code fix proposed yet -- this is a runner/infra condition, and a retry wrapper around checkout would MASK the signal rather than fix it. Minimum viable: teach the reader to tell them apart, which is cheap and already true -- a TLS-infra failure dies in the first ~30s at checkout or the first git command and never prints the guard summary, whereas a real guards failure gets past checkout and prints `PASS n / FAIL n` plus a named failing guard. If it recurs beyond this window, consider `actions/checkout` with a retry, but only with the failure still SURFACED (e.g. an annotation) so a masked flake cannot read as a clean pass.
items.resolution_criteria: Either (a) a week with no further TLS-verify failures, closing it as a transient GitHub incident with the date range recorded; or (b) if it persists, a documented way for a session to distinguish infra-red from real-red WITHOUT opening the job log, since opening the log is the step a rushed session skips.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: No repo-side mitigation was found — no retry/classify step for TLS failures in .github/workflows/guards.yml or pytest-collect.yml, and nothing distinguishes a checkout/network failure from a guard failure in the reported conclusion. The row's own what_to_check (was this a GitHub-side incident?) requires githubstatus.com history, which I cannot reach from this session. — needs live data: githubstatus.com incident history for 2026-08-11 ~22:40-00:00Z, plus a count of TLS-failure job conclusions since. Largely outside this repo's control — the actionable Tier-1 half is making a transport failure distinguishable from a real red, e.g. a post-job step that inspects the failing step's log for the TLS signature and annotates the run. Ending condition: either a recorded 'GitHub incident, no repo action' disposition, or that annotation shipping.

Re-validated: a collapsed state (infra TLS flake indistinguishable from a real failure). Not observed on this session's 3 system-action runs (all exit 0) or 2 CI runs, so no new instance — absence over 5 runs is not evidence it is fixed.

items.title: trainer-vm-diag reported an 'infrastructure failure … VM down or the command exited non-zero' for a run where the SSH succeeded, the command succeeded, and ONLY the result-comment POST failed — and the successful output was discarded
items.source:
Observed on trainer-vm-diag issue #8781 / run 31522478485, 2026-08-11T18:24Z, while measuring the parquet-engine question for BL-20260811-BACKTEST-SIGNAL-CACHE-SILENTLY-INERT-WITHOUT-PARQUET.

POPULATION: 1 of 1 trainer-diag runs dispatched this session failed this way. Small n, but the failure is structural rather than statistical — it is visible in the workflow's own error-handler source, which branches on `CMD_PRESENT` only.

EVIDENCE, from the run log: the job log contains the COMPLETE successful output (venv pyarrow 24.0.0, pandas 3.0.3, '145 parquet files'), immediately followed by `##[error]Unhandled error: HttpError: fetch failed` on the `github.rest.issues.createComment` call. So the command ran to completion on the VM and its result existed; the POST of that result is what failed.
items.description: The relay's failure handler has exactly two branches, keyed on whether a `cmd:` block parsed (`CMD_PRESENT`). Parsed-but-failed therefore always renders as 'this is an infrastructure failure **after** the request was accepted. Likely: VM_SSH_KEY unset/malformed, SSH timeout (trainer VM down or rebooting), or the command itself exited non-zero on the VM.' On this run ALL THREE named causes were false. Worse, the run's actual output — a successful measurement — was left only in the job log, where a reader who believed the comment would never look.
items.why_critical:
This is the THIRD instance of the same class in this relay family, and the workflow's own source contains a long comment explaining the previous two ('A failure message that guesses a cause the run never tested is the same defect class as a diagnostic that mislabels a number', BL-20260730-DIAG-RELAY-FAILURE-COMMENT-MISLEADING). That fix branched on parse-vs-post-parse, which was the right axis for the failure it had seen and is too coarse for this one: it cannot distinguish 'the VM never answered' from 'the VM answered and we could not deliver it'.

The direction of the error is the dangerous part. A session that trusts the comment concludes the TRAINER IS DOWN — which would send it to the trainer-down runbook, or worse, cause it to escalate a healthy VM to the operator as an outage. And the measurement it asked for is silently thrown away, so the natural response is to re-dispatch and pay for it again.
items.next_action: Branch the handler on the actual failure STAGE, not on `CMD_PRESENT` alone — the same fix shape the earlier instance used, applied one level deeper. Concretely: (1) record whether the SSH step succeeded and whether output was captured, and emit a distinct message for 'the command SUCCEEDED but the result could not be posted' that explicitly says the trainer is NOT implicated; (2) always write the captured output to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` before attempting the comment, so a delivery failure can never destroy a successful measurement; (3) retry the createComment once — `fetch failed` is transient — and consider truncating very large bodies, since the failing POST here carried a multi-KB body. Same treatment applies to the sibling vm-diag-snapshot relay, which shares this handler shape.
items.checked: checked: run 31522478485 job log (successful command output present, then HttpError on createComment) and the handler source embedded in that same log, which branches only on CMD_PRESENT. NOT checked: whether vm-diag-snapshot's handler has the identical gap (it looks similar but was not read this session).

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: The failure handler now branches on TWO stages (.github/workflows/trainer-vm-diag.yml:329-357: parse-rejected vs post-SSH), which fixed the sibling defect it cites — but not this one. A run where SSH and the command both succeeded and only the result-comment POST failed still lands in the `parsed === true` branch and reads 'this is an infrastructure failure after the request was accepted. Likely: VM_SSH_KEY unset/malformed, SSH timeout (trainer VM down or rebooting), or the command itself exited non-zero on the VM.' And the output is still discarded on the issues path: the `Upload artifact` step (:283-291) is gated on `github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'`.

resolution_criteria AUTHORED. This row was one of 70 open rows that could never be retired because nothing said what would retire it (BL-20260825-KEPT-OPEN-ROWS-WITH-NO-EXIT-CONDITION-CAN-NEVER-BE-RETIRED). The criterion is derived from THIS row's own recorded material, not from a template - 53 of the 70 carry no material and are deliberately left for genuine authorship rather than given a generic exit condition, which would be the same defect wearing a criteria field.

Re-validated: diagnostic-provenance sub-class A — a failure message naming a cause no code path tested. The system-actions workflow already branches on failure STAGE (I read that logic today); the trainer relay should copy it.

items.resolution_criteria: trainer-vm-diag branches on the failure STAGE, not on CMD_PRESENT: a run whose SSH and command both succeeded but whose comment POST failed emits a message that explicitly states the trainer is NOT implicated; the captured output is written to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY BEFORE the comment is attempted (so a delivery failure can never destroy a successful measurement); and createComment retries once. Verified by exercising the post-failure path - a run or a workflow-level test - NOT by reading the YAML, since the defect is precisely that the YAML reads correct. The sibling vm-diag-snapshot relay carries the same treatment or a recorded reason it does not.

items.title: backtest_system's signal-stream cache write is `except: pass`, so with no parquet engine `--prebuild-cache` is a documented flag that does nothing — silently, and the run just takes ~6x longer
items.source:
Found while running the BL-20260811 flip-override walk-forward in the session sandbox.

POPULATION / MEASUREMENT (sandbox): one walkforward_flip_policy run, 4mem roster x 2 folds x 2 halves = 16 (strategy, window) precache targets, over ~25 minutes on 2026-08-11. 0 of 16 parquet files were written and the signals dir was empty afterwards. Neither pyarrow nor fastparquet importable. Nothing said so.

BLAST RADIUS — MEASURED 2026-08-11, and it is MUCH NARROWER than this row first assumed:
  * TRAINER VM: NOT AFFECTED. `.venv/bin/python3` has pyarrow 24.0.0 + pandas 3.0.3, and runtime_logs/system_backtest/signals holds 145 parquet files (newest 2026-08-02). The cache demonstrably works there. (System python3 3.10.12 lacks pyarrow AND pandas, but research runs use the venv.) Measured via trainer-diag #8781.
  * HARNESSES: only scripts/backtest_system.py uses this parquet cache. backtest_ict_scalp.py, backtest_trend.py, build_backtest_panel.py, build_research_panel.py and run_backtest_vwap.py have zero to_parquet/read_parquet references and none import backtest_system.
  * CI RUNNERS: exactly ONE workflow runs backtest_system.py — c1-conviction-ab.yml — and it installs `pyyaml pandas numpy requests`, with no parquet engine. That is the whole CI exposure.
  * requirements-backtest.txt:18 DOES declare pyarrow>=14.0.0, and 0 workflows install that file.
items.description: scripts/backtest_system.py::generate_signal_stream wraps its `out.to_parquet(cache)` in a bare `except Exception: pass`. Declining to abort is correct — caching IS an optimization — but going fully silent means `--prebuild-cache` reports nothing while doing nothing, and each of the run's 24 cells then re-derives all 4 streams: 96 generations instead of 16, roughly a 6x cost multiplier on a run already measured in hours. The read side has the same broad except, so a corrupt cache file is equally silent.
items.why_critical:
Downgraded in scope by measurement, kept open for the residue. No result is WRONG, only slower, and the trainer — where the operator's real sweeps run — is clean, so the alarming version of this ('every sweep ever run there paid a 6x multiplier') is DISPROVEN and must not be repeated.

What remains is real but small: c1-conviction-ab.yml is the deployable-evidence A/B whose result CLAUDE.md cites for the M16 conviction-sizing decision, and it has been running with an inert cache. Its two arms share the same (symbol, window) signal streams, so a working cache would let arm 2 reuse arm 1's work; without it arm 2 regenerates. That is roughly a 2x cost on the signal-generation half — NOT the 6x seen in the 24-cell walk-forward, and the distinction matters because the workflow's own header reasons carefully about run duration ('each pass over 730d of 5m bars is ~25m') and that budgeting was calibrated against regenerate-every-time behaviour.

The durable lesson is the SILENCE, not the cost: a declared dependency file that no workflow installs, plus a bare `except: pass`, meant the condition was undetectable from the outside and differed per environment while looking identical.
items.next_action:
DONE this session: (a) the write path warns once per process, naming the exception and the remedy; (b) c1-conviction-ab.yml now installs pyarrow; (c) flip-override-walkforward.yml installs it from the start; (d) trainer + CI exposure measured and recorded above, so this is no longer open-ended.

STILL OPEN: (1) the READ path has the same bare except, so a corrupt/partial parquet is silently regenerated rather than reported — same class, unfixed; (2) requirements-backtest.txt is declared but installed by NO workflow, which is how this drifted in the first place — either wire it into the research workflows or delete it, because a dependency manifest nothing reads is worse than none; (3) consider asserting cache effectiveness in the harness (e.g. report cache hits/misses in the run summary) so an inert cache is visible in the OUTPUT, not just in a warning nobody reads.
items.checked: checked 2026-08-11: trainer venv pyarrow 24.0.0 + 145 cached parquet files (trainer-diag #8781); the 6 harness scripts grepped for parquet use; all 7 backtest-running workflows grepped for a parquet engine install; requirements-backtest.txt:18 declares pyarrow and no workflow installs it. NOT checked: whether the read path has ever actually hit a corrupt parquet in practice.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: scripts/backtest_system.py:336-357 replaced the bare swallow with a once-per-process WARNING that names the exception type, states the consequence ('every cell re-derives every stream') and the remedy ('install a parquet engine (pip install pyarrow) to make --prebuild-cache real'), with the measured 0-of-16 incident recorded in the comment at :342-346. The `_CACHE_WRITE_WARNED` global keeps it to one line per run rather than per call.

items.source:
/api/diag/tick_cost, single payload generated 2026-08-11T14:23:18Z, pulled via the diag relay (issue #8771) while re-reading BL-20260810-TICK-CHAIN-260S-PER-TICK.

POPULATION: n=3 ticks, ONE process (process_started_utc 2026-08-11T14:15:35Z, so ~8 minutes of its life), 16 wrapped hooks of which 2 are top-level and 14 are `monitor.*` children, hook_names_refused 0 (so the hook table is complete, not truncated).

The defect itself does NOT depend on that population — it is an identity in the emitted payload's own arithmetic (parents + children = the reported attributed sum, to 0.3ms), so it would hold at any n. The population is stated because the accompanying TIMING figures quoted in what_to_check (mean 114311.2ms / max 128032.9ms) very much do depend on it, and 3 cold-cache ticks is not a distribution.
items.title: tick_cost `attributed_pct` reads 136.8% - it sums PARENT and CHILD hooks, so the field CLAUDE.md calls load-bearing is not a coverage figure and its documented reading yields a negative
items.what_to_check:
MEASURED, and confirmed by arithmetic rather than by reading the code - the sums close to 0.3ms, so this is not an interpretation.

Live payload 2026-08-11T14:23:18Z: mean_ms 114311.2, hooks_attributed_mean_ms 156395.0, attributed_pct 136.8, hook_names_refused 0, ticks_measured 3.

The hook table is NESTED, not a partition:
  top-level    run_one_tick 68108.4 + order_monitor 44247.9 = 112356.3  (vs tick mean 114311.2)
  children     the 14 `monitor.*` entries sum to 44038.4, which is 99.5% of the `order_monitor` PARENT
  all summed   112356.3 + 44038.4 = 156394.7  ==  the reported hooks_attributed_mean_ms 156395.0

So `hooks_attributed_mean_ms` adds every parent to its own children. attributed_pct is therefore 136.8% - a 'coverage' that exceeds 100%.

CLAUDE.md documents this field as: '**`attributed_pct` is the load-bearing field** - the wraps are deliberately COARSE (`run_one_tick` + `order_monitor` only), so `100 - attributed_pct` is every other hook COMBINED.' Applied to the live value that reads -36.8%, which is not a quantity. Two things are now false: the parenthetical (there are 16 wrapped hooks, not 2 - the `monitor.*` layer was added later) and the subtraction.

The TRUE unattributed share is computable and small: 114311.2 - 112356.3 = 1954.9ms = 1.7%.
items.why_critical:
This is the diagnostic-provenance class the instrument was built to be trusted against, occurring IN the instrument. `tick_cost` exists because 'each hook is individually bounded and documented as cheap; nothing measured the SUM' - and the field that reports how much of the sum is accounted for is itself wrong, in the direction that makes coverage look MORE complete than it is. A reader who trusts the documented reading concludes the instrumentation over-covers the tick and stops looking for unwrapped hooks.

SCOPE OF THE DEFECT, checked rather than assumed: `pct_of_total` is NOT affected. It is computed against `mean_ms`, verified across five hooks (run_one_tick 68108.4/114311.2 = 59.58 -> reported 59.6; order_monitor 38.71 -> 38.7; strategy_monitor_loop 17.18 -> 17.2; reconcile_open_trades 4.49 -> 4.5; check_broker_naked_equity_positions 4.07 -> 4.1). Had it used the attributed sum those would read 43.55 / 28.29 / 12.56 / 3.28 / 2.98. So each hook's share IS individually correct against the tick - the defect is confined to `hooks_attributed_mean_ms` and the `attributed_pct` derived from it. The per-hook percentages do still SUM to 136.8% for the same nesting reason, which a reader adding the column up will trip over.

Severity high rather than medium because a wrong coverage figure on a measurement surface is worse than no figure: it is the 'unasserted denominator' sub-class, and the whole point of shipping attributed_pct was to stop exactly that.
items.next_action: In `src/runtime/tick_cost.py`, make the nesting explicit rather than flattening it. Either (a) track hook DEPTH and attribute only top-level hooks into `hooks_attributed_mean_ms`, keeping the `monitor.*` rows as a child breakdown under their parent, or (b) rename the field to something that is true of what it computes and publish a separate, correct `unattributed_pct`. Prefer (a): the question the operator actually asked ('where does the tick time go') needs the tree, not a flat list. Then fix the CLAUDE.md sentence, which is wrong on both the hook count and the subtraction. Add a regression test asserting attributed_pct <= 100 for a nested wrap - the current suite (tests/test_tick_cost.py) does not, which is why this shipped.
items.checked: checked: /api/diag/tick_cost live payload 2026-08-11T14:23:18Z (issue #8771); the parent/child sums reconcile to 0.3ms; pct_of_total's base confirmed as mean_ms across five hooks. NOT checked this session: src/runtime/tick_cost.py's writer source (the conclusions above are all derived from the emitted payload's own arithmetic, which is sufficient to establish the defect but not to name the line).
items.description: attributed_pct reports 136.8% because hooks_attributed_mean_ms sums each parent hook together with its own children (the 14 monitor.* rows are children of order_monitor, and sum to 99.5% of it). A coverage figure cannot exceed 100%, and the documented reading '100 - attributed_pct is every other hook COMBINED' yields -36.8%. True unattributed share is 1.7% (1954.9ms of 114311.2ms). Scope is bounded: pct_of_total uses mean_ms as its base and is individually correct, verified on 5 of 16 hooks.
items.resolved_by: PR #8775 (b6d5b8d) -- NOT this row; see resolution note
items.resolution:
FIXED ON MAIN, and the row was already STALE WHEN IT MERGED -- worth recording rather than quietly ticking, because it is a multi-session-coordination miss, not a clean close.

Verified by ordering, not by inference: b6d5b8d (#8775) is the PARENT of 59d4a98 (#8774), and #8774 is the commit that introduced THIS row. So the concurrent session's fix landed before the row describing the defect did. Two sessions read the same live 136.8% payload the same day and both acted on it; the coordination board did not prevent the duplicate.

The landed fix (src/runtime/tick_cost.py::snapshot) sums TOP-LEVEL hooks only, identifying children by a DOTTED NAME (`monitor.foo`), publishes `nested_hooks` so the hierarchy is visible rather than assumed, and carries 3 regression tests (test_attributed_pct_excludes_nested_children, test_flat_block_reports_zero_nested_and_agrees_with_its_hooks, test_a_child_keeps_its_own_share_of_total). CLAUDE.md's /api/diag/tick_cost entry is corrected on both counts (the negative subtraction and the stale 'COARSE (run_one_tick + order_monitor only)' parenthetical).

MY COMPETING FIX (PR #8782, branch claude/tickcost-attributed-pct) tracked nesting by DEPTH rather than by name. It is CLOSED unmerged -- shipping a second implementation of an already-fixed defect is churn, and the merged one is documented and tested. The one real difference is stated here so it is not lost: the dotted-name rule is an unenforced CONVENTION, so a top-level hook whose name happens to contain a dot silently drops out of the coverage denominator (under-reporting -- the safe direction). The merged code names that limit explicitly in its own comment, so this is an accepted trade-off, not an unflagged fragility. Depth-tracking remains on the unmerged branch if the convention ever bites.

items.source: Found while scoping the P2 item 'port the calibrated harnesses onto real strategy code' (design doc 5d, PR #8605). Measured on main @ 87e6c6d.
items.title: TWO divergent copies of backtest_trend.py: the fidelity/calibration pipeline runs the one WITHOUT the M20/M21 levers, while a LIVE Tier-3 lever cites the other as its reference implementation
items.what_to_check:
MEASURED 2026-08-08 on main @87e6c6d. Two files, same basename, same git history (#8467 rolled venue-aware cost onto BOTH, so they are maintained in parallel, not abandoned): scripts/backtest_trend.py (624 lines, 30 distinct flags) and scripts/research/backtest_trend.py (636 lines, 38 flags). NEITHER IS A SUPERSET - they forked in both directions. Diff is 1048 changed lines across only 4 hunks.

ONLY in scripts/research/ (15): --trail-decay-arm-r, --trail-decay-stall-bars, --trail-decay-tight-mult, --giveback-r, --giveback-min-mfe-r, --bank-at-r, --bank-frac, --confirm-bars, --skip-hours, --vol-skip-above-pctl, --vol-skip-below-pctl, --vol-pctl-window, --trail-vol-above-pctl, --trail-vol-below-pctl, --trail-vol-tight-mult.
ONLY in scripts/ (7): --adx-min, --adx-max, --adx-period, --side-filter, --cooldown-bars, --direction-filter, --confidence-sweep.

WHY IT MATTERS, three ways:
(1) scripts/research/regime_debt_matrix.py::build_harness_cmd invokes scripts/backtest_trend.py - the copy WITHOUT the M20/M21 levers. That harness produces backtest_trades.db, the ONLY input to scripts/research/backtest_fidelity_calibrate.py and therefore to the whole P0/P3 earned-trust chain.
(2) Consequently trend_donchian measures faithful=False with omitted_levers = [exit_head_action, exit_head_model, exit_head_threshold, trail_decay_arm_r, trail_decay_tight_mult]. TWO of those five (the trail_decay pair) are NOT unimplemented - they are implemented in the sibling copy the pipeline does not run. Likewise the five entry params the harness 'has no flag for' (confirm_bars, skip_hours, vol_pctl_window, vol_skip_above_pctl, vol_skip_below_pctl) all EXIST as flags in the research copy. So the fidelity deficit is substantially a WIRING fact, not a capability gap.
(3) src/runtime/trail_decay.py - a LIVE Tier-3 lever module - names scripts/research/backtest_trend.py as its 'Harness reference' in its module docstring, as do src/runtime/trail_vol.py and src/units/strategies/trend_donchian.py. So the evidence base for a live order-affecting lever comes from a harness the fidelity pipeline never runs, and the harness the pipeline DOES run cannot express that lever at all. The M20 sweeps (scripts/research/m20_exit_sweep.py, m20_fleet_exit_sweep.py) also target the research copy.

NOT YET FIXED, deliberately. The obvious move - repoint build_harness_cmd at the research copy - is WRONG as-is: it would silently drop --adx-* (which build_harness_cmd actively forwards via adx_flags) and --side-filter (a declared _TREND_LEVER_FLAG), i.e. trade one fidelity hole for another. Convergence to ONE harness is the fix, and it CHANGES BACKTEST NUMBERS, so it must be validated against real candle history - NOT possible in a web sandbox (the committed data/backtest_candles.csv is ~3.5 days and yields 0 trades; the binance_vision fetch is network-blocked). Do this on the trainer, or on a GH runner via research-backtest-augment.yml, with a before/after metrics comparison per leg.
items.proposed_fix: Converge to ONE trend harness (4 hunks). Suggested order: (a) port the 7 scripts/-only flags into scripts/research/backtest_trend.py OR the 15 research/-only flags into scripts/backtest_trend.py - whichever direction the numeric before/after shows is behaviour-preserving for the currently-invoked path; (b) delete the loser and leave a shim or hard-fail import so a third copy cannot reappear; (c) update _TREND_PLAIN/_TREND_LEVER_FLAG in regime_debt_matrix so the newly-expressible levers stop counting as omitted; (d) re-run the augment + calibrator and record whether trend_donchian's fidelity verdict moves. NOTE the exit_head_* trio is a DIFFERENT problem and does not converge away: it needs the model registry at inference, and research-backtest-augment.yml runs on ubuntu-latest (a free runner with no registry). Either run that leg on the trainer or accept that trend_donchian stays approximate - which, post-#8605, means its backtest can never be stamped `calibrated`. That is arguably CORRECT (a backtest omitting a live advisory exit head is not reproducing live), but it should be a stated decision, not an accident. Sibling check: verify whether backtest_pullback.py / backtest_squeeze.py have the same fork (src/runtime/trail_decay.py's docstring also cites scripts/backtest_pullback.py, so at minimum the naming is inconsistent).

items.source: Investigated after a GitHub Actions action-resolution outage (2026-08-06 ~15:39-17:09+ UTC) failed 11 and cancelled 8 of 29 checks on PR #8534, twice, blocking an operator-approved merge for over 90 minutes.
items.title: CI fans out to 29 concurrent jobs per push — turns any partial GitHub Actions degradation into a guaranteed-red PR, and starves our own runner concurrency
items.what_to_check: MEASURED on PR #8534 / commit 426f017 at 17:09Z: 37 check-run records, 29 DISTINCT checks — 3 success, 11 failure, 8 cancelled, 15 STILL QUEUED 42 minutes after trigger. The repo has 129 workflow files, 46 with a pull_request/push trigger, and 91 separate `uses: actions/checkout@v4` declarations. Each guard is its OWN workflow with ONE job, so each is an independent 'Prepare all required actions' -> 'Getting action download info' call AND an independent `fetch-depth: 0` full-history checkout of a large repo. TWO DISTINCT HARMS. (1) MULTIPLICATIVE FAILURE EXPOSURE: a PR is green only if ALL N jobs resolve their actions, so P(green) = (1-p)^N. At N=29 and a per-job resolution failure rate p, P(green) is 55.7% at p=2%, 22.6% at p=5%, 4.7% at p=10%, 0.2% at p=20%. Consolidated to N=4 the same p values give 92.2% / 81.5% / 65.6% / 41.0%. So during even a MILD upstream degradation the current layout essentially cannot produce a green PR, while a consolidated one usually can. (2) RUNNER STARVATION, which is ours alone and independent of the outage: 29 simultaneous job requests exceed the concurrency the plan allocates, so jobs queue — measured soak-doctrine-guard 16:26:24->17:08:14 (41.8 min) and strategy-coverage-guard 16:26:24->17:03:13 (36.8 min). Worse, the queue time appears to count against each job's own `timeout-minutes: 10`: FOUR jobs cancelled at EXACTLY 10.0 min (silent-empty 10.6, layer 10.0, artifact-validity 10.0, secret-scan 10.0) without ever running. NOTE the concurrency-cap number itself is a HYPOTHESIS — I did not query the plan's documented limit; what is MEASURED is the 36-42 minute queueing, which demonstrates starvation whatever the exact cap is.
items.how: Consolidate the per-guard workflows into ONE aggregate job: a single checkout + a single setup-python + pip install of the union of guard deps, then run every scripts/check_*.py sequentially, collecting failures and exiting non-zero once at the end (so one guard failing still reports the others). Of the 33 PR-triggered workflows, 8 are checkout-only and 25 pull a toolchain — but a single job pays that toolchain cost ONCE instead of 25 times. WALL-CLOCK COST IS ~ZERO: individual guards complete in 6-60s and are dominated by their own checkout, so one aggregate job lands around 2-4 min, while pytest-run (~7.5 min measured) remains the critical path either way. SECONDARY WIN: 29 full-history checkouts per push collapse to ~4, which is a direct Actions-minutes saving against the already-tracked MB-20260706-CI-MINUTES concern. OPERATOR-GATED DEPENDENCY: consolidation CHANGES THE REQUIRED STATUS-CHECK NAMES, so branch protection must be updated in the same change or PRs will hang forever waiting on required checks that no longer exist — that settings edit is the operator's, and it must land BEFORE or WITH the merge, not after. Keep pytest-run, pytest-collect and secret-scan as their own jobs (genuinely different toolchains/permissions).
items.disposition_when_verified: Ship the aggregate guard job + the branch-protection update together, then confirm on the next PR that the check count drops from 29 to ~4 and that a subsequent Actions degradation no longer reds the PR. Do NOT weaken any guard's assertions as part of the consolidation — this is purely a packaging change; a guard that stops failing on a real hit has been broken, not consolidated.
