A session planning M20 sees `pending` and schedules a sweep; no sweep it can launch will move the cell. That is the same reader-facing defect as the exit_head_ml u=0 cells (arithmetically unreachable, not un-run), and it is worth the same explicit split. DELIBERATELY NOT DONE HERE: the cells were NOT re-labelled. blocked:no_harness_levers would be WRONG -- the harness has the levers. Inventing a new status to close them would be the cosmetic-cell anti-pattern (BL-20260730-DONCHIAN-COSMETIC-SHORT-CELLS). They stay `pending` because they are genuinely open work.
items.suggested_fix: Generalize m27's ladder_cells() into m20_fleet_exit_sweep.py so exit_ladder is emitted for any family whose harness carries the bank flags (donchian, pullback, scalp), leaving squeeze/fvg at blocked:no_harness_levers on the measured 0-flag basis rather than a hardcoded family list. Then add exit_ladder to the m20-exit-lever-sweep.yml `levers` input so the column closes on FREE RUNNERS with zero trainer contention. Gate before trusting any new verdict: the 45 existing honest_negative cells were measured on the pre-2026-08-10 no-TP geometry, so a regenerated cell is NOT comparable to them without --tp-cap-pct live parity -- re-deriving one known leg and reconciling against its stored verdict is the check that the generalization reproduces the old method.
items.verification_note: Three sibling hypotheses were tested and REFUTED before landing on this one, recorded so nobody re-runs them: (1) duplicate matrix rows hiding a status -- zero duplicates; (2) the matrix row `execution` field stale vs config/strategies.yaml -- zero disagreements once compared against the 47 EFFECTIVE-live legs rather than the 55 DECLARED legs (_declared_legs() returns all declared legs, which is what made the first pass look like a 4-row defect); (3) exit_ladder being n/a for non-ladder-declaring legs -- refuted by the convention, 45 of 52 rows grade it honest_negative including every donchian sibling.
items.resolution_criteria: scripts/research/m20_fleet_exit_sweep.py emits an `exit_ladder` cell for a donchian or pullback leg (i.e. `--levers exit_ladder` is an accepted choice and produces a graded cell, not `no_harness_levers`), AND a run of .github/workflows/m20-exit-lever-sweep.yml with levers=exit_ladder on trend_donchian_sol_prop + trend_donchian_eth_prop returns a status for both cells, AND those two cells in docs/research/exit-refinement-coverage.json are no longer `pending`. REPRODUCTION CHECK required before the new verdicts are trusted: re-derive exit_ladder for one already-verdicted donchian leg (e.g. trend_donchian_eth) and state whether it reconciles with its stored 2026-07-12 honest_negative -- and if it does not, say so rather than overwriting, since the stored row was measured on the pre-2026-08-10 no-TP geometry and a disagreement is expected rather than a failure of the port.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: scripts/research/m20_fleet_exit_sweep.py still has no exit_ladder emission — the only occurrence of the string is the comment at line 338 explaining why the column is absent — and both affected cells are still open: trend_donchian_sol_prop / exit_ladder and trend_donchian_eth_prop / exit_ladder read `pending`. The new scripts/research/m20_ladder_headroom.py (#9584) is a headroom probe, not a cell producer. — Ends when the fleet sweep accepts `--levers exit_ladder` and produces a graded cell for a donchian/pullback leg, a workflow run returns statuses for both prop cells, and a reproduction check against one already-verdicted donchian leg is recorded. Needs a runner and a reconciliation against the pre-2026-08-10 no-TP verdicts, so not a desk edit.
Re-validated: sweepable but no driver emits the column, so 2 open cells cannot close. Written-and-never-read, inverted.

items.title: A cell QUEUED for a Tier-3 ship (ict_scalp_sol_5m/exit_head_ml) has a passing verdict that does not survive re-partitioning; a second cell's recorded status is contradicted by the fresher screen
items.source: the completed 4-arm fold-offset screen of the three 5m scalp legs (16:13:48Z -> 21:10:52Z), compared against the statuses those same legs carry in docs/research/exit-refinement-coverage.json
items.basis: TWO RUNS, DIFFERENT PARAMETERIZATION -- stated because that is what stops this being a simple 'the matrix is stale' claim. MATRIX (E1 re-run 2026-08-13, relay #8963, fold-mode=trades): sol n_oos=800 beats 12/16, avax n_oos=1000 beats 13/20, xrp n_oos=650 beats 9/13. TONIGHT (4 arms, per_leg, tp_geometry=live_parity_uncapped, tp_cap_pct=0.099): sol n_oos=1150 u=23, avax n_oos=1450 u=29, xrp n_oos=1100 u=22 -- a LARGER book and more folds in every case. VERDICTS. ict_scalp_sol_5m: matrix `passed_unshipped` (candidate, awaiting E3 ship, Tier-3); tonight 3 arms candidate + 1 HONEST_NEGATIVE (off12, beats_hard 16->14, u=23 needs beats_hard*3>=46, 42<46). ict_scalp_avax_5m: matrix `honest_negative` (downgraded 2026-08-13 on beats_hard 13/20); tonight candidate in ALL FOUR arms at gate slack +14/+20/+23/+14. ict_scalp_xrp_5m: matrix `passed_unshipped`; tonight candidate 4/4 -- consistent, no action.
items.detail: The sol row is the urgent half: it is sitting in the operator's queue AWAITING A TIER-3 SHIP, and the freshest evidence says its pass is partition-dependent. Shipping a lever whose passing verdict flips to honest_negative when the folds are cut 12 trades later is a decision the operator should get to make WITH that fact, not without it. Note the AUC gives no warning at all -- sol's AUC spread across the four arms is 0.0034, the SMALLEST of the three legs, while both legs that never flipped have spreads over twice that. The avax row is the opposite direction: a cell recorded `honest_negative` that the larger-book screen grades candidate unanimously with comfortable slack. That is not automatically a correction -- more folds can move a beats-ratio either way, and the two runs differ in book size -- but a recorded negative contradicted 4/4 by fresher, larger evidence should not sit unexamined.
items.resolution_criteria: Either (a) both cells are re-graded from ONE agreed parameterization -- same fold-mode, same tp_geometry, same book -- and the matrix records that run with its arm count, so the two runs are no longer being compared across differing inputs; or (b) the matrix cell for ict_scalp_sol_5m carries an explicit note that its verdict was measured partition-dependent (1 of 4 arms honest_negative) so the Tier-3 ship decision is made with it; and in EITHER case the operator has answered the ship question for sol with the flip on the table. Closing this by re-running once and taking whichever verdict comes back does NOT satisfy it -- a single partition is the exact thing the screen showed to be insufficient.
items.deliberately_not_done: No matrix status was changed. Overwriting a recorded verdict with a differently-parameterized run would destroy the disagreement that IS the finding, and ship/unship is Tier-3 regardless.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Both cells are still as filed: ict_scalp_sol_5m/exit_head_ml is `passed_unshipped` (tp_geometry live_parity) and its ref records only the single-run marginality ('beats_hard 16/23 clears by 2 points of 46, so one fold the other way fails it') — the 4-arm screen result (1 of 4 arms honest_negative) is not on the cell; ict_scalp_avax_5m is still `honest_negative` with the counter-evidence recorded and 'QUEUED for the operator'. — Proposed: put both to the operator together — (i) sol's Tier-3 ship decision made WITH the 4-arm flip on the table (and, if it proceeds, the partition-dependence written onto the cell), and (ii) avax's status question given 4/4 candidate on a 45% larger book. Do not re-run once and take whichever verdict returns; a single partition is what the screen showed to be insufficient.
Re-validated: a cell QUEUED for a Tier-3 ship whose verdict does not survive re-partitioning. Should block that ship until reconciled.

RESOLVED on criterion (b), OBSERVED IN THE ARTIFACT 2026-09-02 -- both of its conjuncts, read out of docs/research/exit-refinement-coverage.json (row strategy=ict_scalp_sol_5m, cell exit_head_ml), not inferred from a PR.

The criterion's option (b) reads: 'the matrix cell for ict_scalp_sol_5m carries an explicit note that its verdict was measured partition-dependent (1 of 4 arms honest_negative) so the Tier-3 ship decision is made with it; and in EITHER case the operator has answered the ship question for sol with the flip on the table.'

  (i) THE NOTE IS ON THE CELL, and it cites this row by id: '...its pass does not survive re-partitioning -- the 4-arm screen flips it to honest_negative when folds are cut 12 trades later, and its AUC spread across the arms (0.0034) is the SMALLEST of the three legs, so the AUC gave no warning at all. BL-20260815-SCALP-EXIT-HEAD-MATRIX-DISAGREES-WITH-THE-4-ARM-SCREEN'.
  (ii) THE OPERATOR HAS ANSWERED THE SHIP QUESTION FOR SOL: 'this cell was QUEUED for a Tier-3 ship and the ship is CANCELLED (operator decision 2026-08-23)'. The same entry re-grades the cell passed_unshipped -> blocked while explicitly NOT withdrawing the E1 measurement.

⚠️ ONE CLAUSE I VERIFIED AS RECORDED RATHER THAN AS SEQUENCED. Both facts sit in the SAME dated 2026-08-23 entry, and the primary reason given for the cancellation is that the lever is inert on ict_scalp (no consumer in the unit), with the partition-dependence introduced by 'Beyond being inert'. So the artifact records the decision and the flip together; I cannot establish from it that the operator weighed the flip BEFORE deciding rather than the flip being written alongside. The criterion asks what the cell carries and whether the operator answered, and both are satisfied on the artifact; stating the limit rather than hiding it.

⚠️ THE ROW'S SECOND CELL IS NOT RESOLVED AND IS NOT BEING DROPPED. The criterion's text is sol-only, but the row's TITLE also covers 'a second cell's recorded status is contradicted by the fresher screen' -- ict_scalp_avax_5m, still `honest_negative` today with counter-evidence on the cell reading 'QUEUED for the operator' since 2026-08-14 and never answered. Closing this row silently would lose that, so it is filed as its own row with its own criterion: BL-20260902-AVAX-SCALP-EXIT-HEAD-NEGATIVE-CONTRADICTED-AND-UNANSWERED. Resolved here, carried there.

items.title: send-ping silently delivered `|` for 8 consecutive hourly pings and exited 0
items.source: observed while verifying my own hourly ping actually fired
items.why_it_matters: The issue-body parser for send-ping is `grep -i -m1 '^message:'` -- one line, prefix stripped. A body written `message: |` with an indented block therefore yields the single character `|`; the action queues a 1-character ping and EXITS 0, and the issue closes 'completed'. MEASURED: eight consecutive hourly status pings (#9495 #9499 #9501 #9504 #9507 #9512 #9515 #9521, 16:17Z->23:18Z) each delivered `|`. That is ~7 hours in which the operator's only overnight visibility channel was dead while every signal said success -- during a session the operator had explicitly asked to ping at least hourly. The pre-existing non-empty check cannot catch it because `|` is non-empty. Same class as the 403-poller that read 0 checks as clean: a green that carried nothing, which nobody goes looking behind. Proof of both directions is in the action's own log line: the failing send reported 'Enqueuing low ping to claude bot (1 chars)', the corrected resend (#9523) reported 1279 chars.
items.next_action: FIXED in this session for the bare-marker case: system-actions.yml now refuses `message:` equal to a YAML block marker (| |- |+ > >- >+) with an error naming the single-line parse. REMAINING, and why this row stays open: the guard is enumerative, so it catches the shape that bit us and not the general case of a message that parses SHORTER than the author intended. The durable fix is for the wrapper to assert a plausible length -- or echo the queued body back -- so a truncated ping can never read as a delivered one. Also worth auditing whether `reason:` and other single-line fields have produced the same silent truncation elsewhere.
items.resolution_criteria: A send-ping whose parsed message is materially shorter than the issue body's intended message either fails the action or is visibly reported as truncated in the issue comment; demonstrated by a deliberate multi-line `message: |` dispatch that does NOT close as a clean success.

updates.note: Root-caused, bare-marker guard shipped, and the 23:00Z ping resent single-line and confirmed at 1279 chars. Backlog row kept open for the general truncation case.

[sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: .github/workflows/system-actions.yml:601-606 now refuses a `message:` equal to a bare YAML block marker (| |- |+ > >- >+) with an explicit error, so the exact shape that bit is caught. The general case is not: the parser is still the single-line `grep -i -m1 '^…message…'` at :414-415, there is no plausible-length assertion, and no step echoes the parsed body back into the issue comment — so any other silent truncation still reads as a clean success. — Tier-2 (it gates the operator's notification path). Ends when a materially-truncated parse either fails the action or is visibly reported as truncated, demonstrated by a deliberate multi-line dispatch.

Re-validated; I could not close it. This review's consolidated ping was dispatched via system-action issue #10418 using a PLAIN scalar (not a YAML block scalar), so it does not exercise the failure path. Delivery is also not observable from this session. Keep open; the fix is to reject/normalise a block scalar in the action's parser rather than to rely on callers avoiding it.

items.title: Live tick mean 72.3s -> 140.0s at the same n=40; fetch.1d ~4x its documented cost
items.source: /api/diag/tick_cost via diag relay #9527, one process from 2026-08-15T23:06:29Z
items.why_it_matters: MEASURED, like-for-like at the SAME sample size the last documented read used (ticks_measured=40 both): tick mean_ms 72.3s (2026-08-14, CLAUDE.md) -> 140.0s now, +93.7%, with max_ms 185.6s. That is 2.02x the post-decouple 69.3s, 2.18x the 64.1s recorded after the candle-cache cap raise, and 1.30x the PRE-decouple 107.9s -- the tick is now slower than before M20 decoupled the exit loop, which erases the measured benefit of that work. The tick bounds how stale the price behind a live order is (strategies read close.iloc[-1] as current price), so this is a money-adjacent regression, not just a throughput one. Driver appears to be per-fetch latency rather than cache rate: cache hit rate is 44.8% (831/1853 on-loop), consistent with the 41.5% after the cap raise, while fetch.1d on-loop mean is 14,226ms against the 2.4-3.6s per fetch CLAUDE.md records -- roughly 4x. fetch.1h 5,055ms; fetch.15m 2,746ms on-loop vs 8,506ms off-loop; pipeline.signal_build mean 3,975ms with max 60,405ms.
items.next_action: NOT diagnosed, and two candidate causes are explicitly unmeasured rather than dismissed: (a) the measurement window is a WEEKEND -- the process started 2026-08-15T23:06Z (Saturday night) and the read is from Sunday 2026-08-16 -- while the 72.3s baseline was Friday 2026-08-14, a full trading day. So equity/futures venues were shut for the whole 'now' sample and open for the whole baseline, and part of this may be closed-venue timeouts rather than a code regression. (Corrected 2026-08-16: an earlier version of this row and the board comment said 'today is a Saturday'. It is Sunday; 08-15 was the Saturday. The conclusion is unchanged and slightly strengthened -- the contrast is a full weekend against a weekday, not one day against another) -- re-read /api/diag/tick_cost on a weekday session before concluding anything; (b) a genuine fetch-path or venue-latency change since 08-14. Distinguishing them is one weekday read. Flagged to the tick-chain session on coordination board #6927 (PR #8815 is their scope; this session did not touch it). NOTE what is NOT the cause, checked: the exit-loop decouple IS running (exit_loop_health state=fresh, 241 passes), and exit cadence still clears the operator's 60s ask at max_pass_ms 50.4s.
items.resolution_criteria: A weekday /api/diag/tick_cost read at n>=40 either shows tick mean back near the 72.3s baseline -- in which case this was venue-closure latency and the row closes with that stated -- or confirms the regression persists, in which case fetch.1d's 4x cost is root-caused to a specific change or venue behaviour.

updates.note: Opened from diag #9527. Comparison is like-for-like (n=40 both sides). Flagged on board #6927 for the tick-chain session rather than acted on.

Corrected the day-of-week: the read is SUNDAY 2026-08-16 and the 72.3s baseline is FRIDAY 2026-08-14. Earlier text said 'today is a Saturday'. Numbers, conclusion and resolution criterion are unchanged; the weekend-vs-weekday contrast is now stated accurately rather than approximately.

PARTIAL TEST OF THE VENUE-CLOSURE HYPOTHESIS, from data already in hand rather than waiting for the weekday read. Joined the tick_cost per-timeframe fetch means to the coverage matrix's authoritative strategy->symbol->tf mapping (NOT a hand heuristic -- my first attempt classified via config/strategies.yaml and returned 0 crypto for every timeframe, because strategies carry no `symbol` field; symbols come from account routing). Result, live legs only: 1d 100% equity/futures -> 14,226ms; 1h 55% -> 5,055ms; 15m 25% -> 2,745ms; 5m 0% -> 1,522ms; 2h 0% -> 221ms; 4h 0% -> 199ms. Monotonic in the equity/futures share across 1d/1h/15m, and the two cheapest frames are pure crypto -- consistent with closed venues driving the cost. ⚠️ IT DOES NOT SETTLE IT, and the counter-example is in the same table: 5m is ALSO pure crypto yet costs 1,522ms, ~7x the pure-crypto 2h/4h. So venue class cannot be the whole story and at least one other factor is present. More fundamentally, timeframe is CONFOUNDED with venue class here by construction -- every 1d leg is an equity/ETF -- so this data cannot separate '1d is slow because its venues are shut' from '1d fetches are inherently expensive'. The weekday read remains the discriminator; this only raises the prior.

[sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Purely a live measurement (n=40 weekend read, /api/diag/tick_cost via relay #9527) and its own resolution criterion is a weekday re-read; nothing in the checkout can settle whether 140.0s is venue-closure latency or a regression. The row already records a partial test of the venue hypothesis with an explicit counter-example (5m is pure crypto and still 1,522ms). — needs live data: a weekday /api/diag/tick_cost read at n>=40, reporting mean AND max beside the count. Composes with BL-20260814-TICK-2X-SLOWER-AFTER-IB-PIN — do not close either against the other.

RESOLVED. LIVE RE-MEASUREMENT 2026-08-29, two independent trader processes: process 15:11:25Z n=31 mean 45,467 ms / max 61,467 ms; process 16:10:51Z n=19 mean 47,986 ms / max 59,627 ms. So the tick is ~46-48 s mean / ~60 s max. That is not merely better than the regression this row records — it is BETTER THAN THE M20 BASELINE (69.3 s mean / 96.8 s max) the row measures against. Two processes agreeing at ~47 s against a recorded 140-148.7 s is a 3x gap, far outside per-process sampling noise. ⚠️ State the population: both reads are per-PROCESS and n is small (31, 19), so the MAX is systematically under-observed — that limitation is itself BL-20260816-TICK-COST-MAX-RESETS-EVERY-DEPLOY, which stays open. The MEAN is what this row is about and it has recovered. Per-hook split on the 16:10:51Z process: run_one_tick 28,896 ms mean (60.2%), order_monitor 17,961 ms (37.4%), attributed_pct 97.6. fetch.1d does not appear in the top hooks at all, so the '~4x its documented cost' half of this row is also not reproducing.

items.title: Both M21 entry sweeps drop the live TP cap; the M21 matrix has 27 DECISION cells and no geometry tracking
items.source: grep over scripts/research/*.py + docs/research/entry-refinement-coverage.json, read this session
items.why_it_matters: VERIFIED: scripts/research/m21_entry_sweep.py:133 and scripts/research/m21_entry_head_round.py:125 both call base_args(name, cfg, fam, data, resample) POSITIONALLY, so tp_cap_pct defaults to 0.0 and base_args appends neither --tp-cap-pct nor --tp-r for a family in LIVE_TP_CAPPED_FAMILIES. That is the identical defect this session just fixed in m20_flip_replay_sweep.py, and all three are the 'THREE SIBLING SWEEPS' of BL-20260814-THREE-SIBLING-SWEEPS-STILL-BUILD-NO-TAKE-PROFIT-BOOKS-AND-STAMP-NOTHING; the M20 one is now done and these two are what remains of it. WHY IT IS WORSE HERE THAN IT WAS IN M20: the regime_flip_exit column that motivated the M20 fix is 38 cells and ALL 38 are honest_negative, so its stale evidence costs knowledge only. docs/research/entry-refinement-coverage.json carries 23 'shipped' and 4 'passed_unshipped' -- 27 DECISION cells -- and many of its rows plainly name donchian and pullback legs, which ARE capped families. A shipped entry decision taken on a book with no take-profit is the money-adjacent version of this defect. AND M21 HAS NO GEOMETRY TRACKING AT ALL: the matrix has no tp_geometry field and there is no m21 equivalent of m20_coverage_rollup's evidence_vintage / LEVER_GEOMETRY_CUTOVER, so nothing anywhere reports that this column's evidence is conditioned on the wrong geometry -- the M20 side at least SAYS so via its NEVER sentinel.
items.not_established: I did NOT establish how many of the 27 decision cells sit on capped families, and an earlier draft of this note said 25 -- that figure was WRONG and is recorded here so it is not re-quoted. It came from running m20_fleet_exit_sweep.classify() over the matrix's `strategy` values, but 5 of the 15 M21 rows are COMPOSITE labels covering many legs at once (e.g. 'equities 1d fleet (spy/qqq/... trend; gld/tlt/... pullback)', which mixes both families in one row), so classify() was substring-guessing on strings it was never designed for. A real count needs M21's own row->leg mapping, which I did not read. Separately noticed while listing the rows: 'xauusd_trend_1h' appears as its own row AND inside 'xauusd_trend_1h / mgc_trend_1h', so at least one leg is double-counted -- its own small defect, unmeasured here.
items.next_action: (1) Apply the M20 fix to both files: add --tp-cap-pct defaulting to 0.099 and pass it as the 6th positional to base_args. The geometry-stamp derivation is now a shared function, m20_fleet_exit_sweep.tp_geometry_for (extracted 2026-08-16), so both should stamp via that rather than re-deriving -- a third copy is how the 2026-08-10 fleet-sweep fix failed to reach its siblings in the first place. (2) Establish the real capped-family denominator over the 27 decision cells using M21's own row->leg mapping, and split the composite rows if that mapping does not exist. (3) Decide whether M21 needs an evidence-vintage surface; today nothing reports that these cells are conditioned on a no-take-profit book. None of this is Tier-3: the sweeps are research tooling and the remedy is re-measurement, not a config change. But re-measurement may move a 'shipped' entry cell, and THAT adjudication is the operator's.
items.resolution_criteria: ALL THREE, each observable: (1) `grep -n 'resample)' scripts/research/m21_entry_sweep.py scripts/research/m21_entry_head_round.py` returns NO base_args call — both pass a 6th positional tp_cap_pct — AND each file's --tp-cap-pct argparse default is 0.099, mirroring m20_flip_replay_sweep.py; (2) an M21 sweep run emits `tp_geometry: live_parity_capped` for a donchian/pullback leg, produced by calling m20_fleet_exit_sweep.tp_geometry_for rather than a re-derived label — the same A/B that verified the M20 fix (relay #9534) shows the capped and uncapped arms differ in TRADE COUNT, not just in verdict, which is what proves the cap reached the harness; (3) the count this row could not establish is established: the number of the 27 M21 decision cells (23 shipped + 4 passed_unshipped) that sit on a LIVE_TP_CAPPED_FAMILIES leg, derived from M21's own row->leg mapping and NOT from classify() over the matrix's composite `strategy` labels. A restated figure with no stated mapping does not close this.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Criterion (1) is MET (commit 8a23a72): scripts/research/m21_entry_sweep.py:142 and m21_entry_head_round.py:130 both pass `a.tp_cap_pct` as the 6th positional to base_args, and both declare `--tp-cap-pct` with default=0.099 (:104 and :96 respectively), stamping geometry via the shared tp_geometry_for. Criteria (2) and (3) are unmet: no M21 run artifact proves the capped/uncapped arms differ in trade count, and docs/research/entry-refinement-coverage.json contains ZERO occurrences of 'tp_geometry', so the capped-family denominator over the 27 decision cells is still unestablished. — needs a sweep run for (2); (3) needs M21's own row->leg mapping (5 of 15 rows are composite labels, and xauusd_trend_1h appears twice), which must not be re-derived with classify() over the composite strings.
Re-validated: third driver with the positional-base_args defect. See BL-20260814-THREE-SIBLING-SWEEPS-STILL-BUILD-NO-TAKE-PROFIT-BOOKS-AND-STAMP-NOTHING for the consolidated fix.

items.source: Found by artifact-validity-guard turning red repo-wide at 2026-08-16T05:48Z on PR #9549 (a one-file config diff touching nothing macro). The expired entry was comms/macro/econ_calendar_captures/US-20260729T073711Z.fmp.json, owner BL-20260730-PRODUCER-VACUITY-GUARD, until 2026-08-15. That owner row had been marked `resolved` on 2026-08-01 — 15 days before the expiry fired.
items.title: [tooling] KNOWN_VACUOUS attribution is satisfied by a backlog id that may already be CLOSED — the 'owner' of live debt can be a row nobody is watching
items.description: check_artifact_validity.known_vacuous_problems enforces that every KNOWN_VACUOUS entry NAMES a backlog row and carries an unexpired `until`. It does not check that the named row is still OPEN. So the guard's stated purpose — 'every entry MUST name a backlog id, so the debt is owned, not hidden' — is satisfied only syntactically: a resolved row owns nothing. Worked instance: the FMP capture entry named BL-20260730-PRODUCER-VACUITY-GUARD, resolved 2026-08-01 on the grounds that the GUARD shipped; the artifact that entry grandfathered stayed vacuous, and the debt surfaced not as a review item but as a repo-wide CI outage on an unrelated PR two weeks later. Note the failure was still CAUGHT — the `until` expiry is the backstop and it did its job; what failed is the intended EARLIER signal (an owned, open row a review session would drain). Same family as the presence-only `# data-wiring:` marker lesson in CLAUDE.md: a guard that checks a string is PRESENT rather than that it MEANS something is cheaper to satisfy than to honour. FIX: have known_vacuous_problems resolve each `backlog` id against docs/claude/*-review-backlog.json and fail when the id is unknown (a typo'd id currently passes too) or its status is not open/snoozed. Cheap — the backlogs are committed JSON in the same repo, so no network and no new dependency.
items.trigger_condition: A KNOWN_VACUOUS (or equivalent grandfather-list) entry names a backlog id that is resolved, or that does not exist in any review backlog.
items.resolution_criteria: (1) known_vacuous_problems resolves every entry's `backlog` id against the committed review backlogs and reports a problem when the id is unknown or its status is not open/snoozed; (2) a plant-proven self-test covers BOTH the unknown-id and the closed-id cases, plus a positive control showing an open id still passes; (3) the guard is clean against the current KNOWN_VACUOUS list (empty as of 2026-08-16, so the self-test is what carries the proof, not the live run).

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: scripts/ops/check_artifact_validity.py::known_vacuous_problems (lines 166-186) checks only that an entry HAS a `backlog` value and an unexpired `until` — it never opens docs/claude/*-review-backlog.json, so a typo'd id and a resolved id both pass. Exactly as filed. — Tier-1 CI; cheap (the backlogs are committed JSON in the same repo, no network).

Re-validated: an 'owner' of live debt that may be a closed row. Directly relevant to this triage — I resolved 17 rows today, and any KNOWN_VACUOUS entry pointing at one of them is now vacuous. Worth re-running that check after this PR merges.

items.tier: 1 (measurement); any cadence or fetch change touching the exit loop is Tier-2
items.title: The exit-evaluation interval has BREACHED the 60s requirement (max 61.04s, 2 breaches) — escalated 2026-08-18 from 'crept to 58.9s, 1.1s under'
items.detail:
MEASURED 2026-08-16T05:39:18Z, /api/diag/tick_cost, n=694 passes from one process (started 2026-08-15T23:06:29Z): offloop_hooks.monitor.strategy_monitor_loop mean 28852.0ms, max 58940.8ms.

WHY THE MAX IS THE BINDING NUMBER, not the mean. EXIT_LOOP_INTERVAL_SECONDS is period-TARGETING (slack = interval - elapsed), so the interval between two exit evaluations is max(interval, pass) = max(30s, pass). A 58.9s pass therefore means a live trade went 58.9s without re-evaluation. The operator's stated requirement - the thing M20 was built for - is that no live trade goes more than 60s without evaluation. That leaves 1.1s of margin.

IT HAS BEEN MOVING IN ONE DIRECTION. M20 shipped documenting a 22.4s mean and was live-verified at 30.2s observed / 34.1s worst, described as clearing the 60s ask by 43.1%. A warm re-measure on 2026-08-14 read 26.6s mean at n=219. This read is 28.9s mean / 58.9s max at n=694. The mean has drifted ~29% above the documented baseline and the MAX has grown 73% since go-live verification.

BL-20260814-EXIT-PASS-SLOWER-THAN-M20 was closed on the warm re-measure, which looked settled at the time; it did not track the max, and the max is the quantity the requirement is written against.

THE PASS IS FETCH-BOUND, so this is the same root as the tick regression (BL-20260814-TICK-2X-SLOWER-AFTER-IB-PIN): off-loop fetchby.strategy_monitor_loop is n=10034 - the largest fetch consumer anywhere - and off-loop fetch.1d is mean 10720.9ms over n=1073. A TTL or fetch change aimed at the tick reaches EXIT decisions too, in both directions.

NOTHING WATCHES THIS. exit_loop_health grades the loop fresh/stale on EXIT_LOOP_STALE_SECONDS (default 180s) - it answers 'is the loop alive', not 'is the interval inside the requirement'. A pass at 59s is 'fresh'. So the requirement can be breached without any surface saying so; it is only visible by reading max_pass_ms out of tick_cost by hand, which is how this was found.

--- 2026-08-16, follow-up session: CRITERION 4 SETTLED, CRITERION 2 SHIPPED ---

THE ~29000ms CEILING IS A TIMEOUT, NOT LATENCY. It is _IB_FETCH_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_S
(src/exchange/ib_connector.py:113), which is DERIVED, not chosen:
    _IB_FETCH_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_S = IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S * 3.0 + 5.0
and IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S is <unset> on the live VM in BOTH the running process and
the declared env (get-env, issue #9570, 2026-08-16T06:35Z), so the 8.0 code default
applies and the operative value is EXACTLY 29.0s. Three independent timeframes were
observed maxing at 29000.5 / 29000.3 / 29000.4 ms (fetch.1h, fetch.1d, off-loop
fetch.15m) - three frames landing on one constant to within 0.5 ms.

WHAT THAT CHANGES. A fetch that hits it returned None. So those samples are a
FAILURE population sitting inside the same fetch.* mean as successful fetches, and
the mean is not the quantity it appears to be. More importantly the approach to 60s
is QUANTISED rather than gradual: one queue timeout is 48.3% of the 60s exit budget
and two are 96.7%. The worst observed pass, 58940.8ms, is 2 x 29000 + 941.

RESIDUAL, STATED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED OVER: no 'timed out waiting for the pinned IB
thread' warning line was captured. The n=694 process is gone (the trader restarted
2026-08-16T06:24Z) and the journalctl relay truncates to a 55000-byte comment budget
- a 7h window request returned 55KB of 452KB, covering 94 SECONDS. An early zero-count
over that slice was discarded rather than reported: it had no denominator. The
identification rests on the arithmetic + the live constant, not on a captured firing.

CRITERION 2 IS SHIPPED. exit_loop_health now MEASURES the completion-to-completion
interval (not the max(interval, pass) derivation - a stall between the sleep and the
next completion is invisible to the derivation and visible to the measurement) and
grades it against a separate EXIT_EVAL_MAX_INTERVAL_SECONDS (default 60.0), with a
four-state requirement_state - within / breached / not_measured / unknown - registered
with collapsed-state-guard. `fresh` and `breached` can now coexist, which is the exact
condition that was previously unrepresentable. A breach alerts once per PROCESS
(max_interval_ms resets on restart, so a global latch would have gone silent after the
first breach ever - and there were three processes in the 2026-08-15/16 window alone).

CRITERION 1 IS PARTIAL. Second process observed: started 2026-08-16T06:24:32Z,
max_pass_ms 40872.5 at n=11 passes (exit_loop_health, read 06:30:00Z) - 68% of the
requirement within six minutes of a cold start. That is a second data point, not a
trend; it needs re-reads once the new instrumentation is deployed.

--- CRITERION 1 ANSWERED: 'trending one way' DOES NOT HOLD ---

Second process, sampled twice: started 2026-08-16T06:24:32Z, max_pass_ms 40872.5ms
at n=11 and 41543.5ms at n=38. The max moved 1.6% across a 3.5x increase in samples
and sits at 69% of the requirement, not approaching it.

TWO METHODOLOGICAL FAULTS IN THE ORIGINAL SERIES, which this row and PR #9560 both
asserted and which I repeated before checking:

1. IT MIXES MEANS AND MAXIMA AS IF THEY WERE ONE QUANTITY. Separated:
     means : 22.4s (n=55) -> 30.2s (go-live) -> 26.6s (n=219) -> 28.9s (n=694)
             -> 21.6s (n=32, process B). Range 21.6-30.2s, up-down-up-down.
             NOT a trend. The mean is flat and process B is the LOWEST of the five.
     maxima: 34.1s (go-live) -> 58.9s (n=694) -> 41.5s (n=38). THREE points.
2. IT COMPARES MAXIMA ACROSS DIFFERENT n. A maximum grows with sample size even
   from a fixed distribution, so max(n=694) > max(n=38) is the EXPECTED result of
   drawing more samples, not evidence of degradation. The row's own criterion 1
   warned the series was 'built from four different sample sizes and is only
   suggestive'; the correct conclusion is stronger than 'suggestive' - as a TREND
   claim it is unsupported.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is still worth the work: 58940.8ms was REALLY OBSERVED. A live
trade did go 58.9s without re-evaluation. The honest diagnosis is not 'the system is
degrading toward the requirement' but 'the n=694 process was the first sample large
enough to see a tail that may have been there since go-live' - which is a DIFFERENT
problem with a different fix. Degradation would argue for finding what is getting
slower; a fat tail argues for bounding the tail, i.e. the 29.0s queue-timeout seam in
BL-20260816-IB-QUEUE-TIMEOUT-EXCEEDS-EXIT-BUDGET.

SUPPORTING CONTRAST, on how to tell a timeout from latency in this data: process B's
maxima cluster near 26.6s (26654.1 / 26654.2 / 26643.8 / 26496.5) with a spread of
157.7ms, whereas the 29.0s cluster spread 0.2ms across three frames. A timeout is
tight to sub-millisecond; latency is not. The 26.6s group is real latency and no
queue timeout fired anywhere in process B.

--- THIRD PROCESS, 2026-08-16T07:46Z: the tail reading holds, and a NEW caveat ---

Process C started 2026-08-16T07:34:25Z (deploy git_sha 8a23a72b; process B is gone).
At n=23 its max_pass_ms is 47449.6ms - 79.1% of the requirement. Four samples now:
    A 2026-08-15T23:06:29Z  n=694  58940.8ms  98.2%
    B 2026-08-16T06:24:32Z  n= 11  40872.5ms  68.1%
    B 2026-08-16T06:24:32Z  n= 38  41543.5ms  69.2%
    C 2026-08-16T07:34:25Z  n= 23  47449.6ms  79.1%
Within B the max moved +1.6% across 3.5x the samples. BETWEEN processes, C at n=23
already exceeds B at n=38 - so the spread is process-to-process variance plus
extreme-value growth in n, not a march along the calendar. The tail reading holds.

NEW CAVEAT, and it limits the instrumentation this session shipped: THE TRADER
RESTARTS OFTEN - three processes in ~8.5h (23:06 -> 06:24 -> 07:34), because
ict-git-sync auto-deploys every merge to main and main is busy. max_interval_ms and
max_pass_ms are PER-PROCESS and reset on each deploy, while the tail needs a large n
to be sampled at all - process A only reached n=694 because it ran through a quiet
overnight window. So on a busy day the requirement grade will systematically
UNDER-report: requirement_state can read `within` all day simply because no process
lived long enough to draw the tail.

Per-process is still the correct SCOPE (a max cannot be pooled across processes
without pooling their distributions, and the alert has to reset or it goes silent
forever). But a reader must not read `within` as 'the requirement was met today' -
it means 'not breached in the samples this process drew'. Read it beside
intervals_measured, exactly as max_multiple is read beside measured_n on the exposure
soak. If a cross-process view is ever wanted it needs a durable accumulator, which is
a different design and is NOT what shipped.

--- ESCALATION 2026-08-18T06:45Z (system-review session) ---
`/api/diag/log_file?name=exit_loop_health` now reports `requirement_state: "breached"`, NOT `within`:
  passes 819 | intervals_measured 818 | process_started_utc 2026-08-17T23:03:42Z
  max_interval_ms 61035.9 @ 2026-08-17T23:07:31Z | interval_breaches 2 | last_breach 2026-08-18T04:21:16Z
  max_pass_ms 60204.3 | last_pass_ms 40870.6 | state fresh | stale_threshold_s 180 | requirement_s 60
So a live trade went 61.0s without exit evaluation, twice, on a single 7.7h process at n=818 — a sample large enough that this is the tail being drawn, not a short-window artifact. Note `state: "fresh"` and `requirement_state: "breached"` coexisting, exactly the condition the two-threshold split was built to represent. Mean interval is ~33.9s, so the mean remains comfortable and only the MAX breaches — which is why a mean-only reading kept this looking healthy.
The predecessor entry's diagnosis (a fat tail on a fetch-bound pass, not a system-wide slowdown) is unchanged and is now supported by an actual breach rather than a near-miss. | STATUS NORMALISED 2026-08-22 (workplan 0.1 Step 0): the free-text status 'open_breached_measured' was collapsed to 'open' so the open set is countable. The original wording is preserved here verbatim; the mapping failed TOWARD open wherever the text signalled remaining work.
items.resolution_criteria:
1. ANSWERED 2026-08-16 - it is a TAIL, not a trend, and the original series was not valid evidence of one (it mixed means with maxima, and compared maxima across different n where a max grows with n mechanically). See the detail. Residual work is to keep sampling max_interval_ms per process, but the 'creeping toward 60s' framing should not be repeated.
SUPERSEDED:  Two processes now: 2026-08-15T23:06Z n=694 max 58940.8ms; 2026-08-16T06:24Z n=11 max 40872.5ms. Needs re-reads of the NEW max_interval_ms across several more processes, always stating n and process start.
2. DONE 2026-08-16 - exit_loop_health carries measured max_interval_ms + a four-state requirement_state graded against EXIT_EVAL_MAX_INTERVAL_SECONDS (60s), and a breach alerts once per process. Verify live once deployed: requirement_state must be present on /api/diag/log_file?name=exit_loop_health.
3. Unchanged - do NOT lower EXIT_LOOP_INTERVAL_SECONDS.
4. DONE - the ceiling is _IB_FETCH_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_S = 29.0s exactly (IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S unset live -> 8.0 default -> *3+5). See the detail. The follow-on design question is split out to BL-20260816-IB-QUEUE-TIMEOUT-EXCEEDS-EXIT-BUDGET.

updates.note:
MONITORED ACROSS SIX PROCESSES, and the new instrumentation is verified in production.

  process started        n     max_ms    %req   field
  2026-08-15T23:06:29Z   694   58940.8   98.2%  max_pass_ms
  2026-08-16T06:24:32Z    11   40872.5   68.1%  max_pass_ms
  2026-08-16T06:24:32Z    38   41543.5   69.2%  max_pass_ms
  2026-08-16T07:34:25Z    23   47449.6   79.1%  max_pass_ms
  2026-08-16T08:34:15Z     4   18691.4   31.2%  max_pass_ms
  2026-08-16T09:07:09Z    16   47196.3   78.7%  max_INTERVAL_ms (the new field, live)

ZERO breaches observed across all six. The tail reading holds: no process other than the n=694 overnight one has come near 60 s, and the spread between processes at similar n (47449.6 at n=23 vs 41543.5 at n=38) is variance plus extreme-value growth, not calendar drift.

CROSS-CHECK that the new field measures what it claims: on the 09:07 process max_interval_ms 47196.3 vs max_pass_ms 47195.5 — a delta of 0.8 ms, exactly the max(30s, pass) relationship the design predicts when pass > 30 s. And intervals_measured 15 against passes 16 (n passes yield n−1 intervals) confirms the not_measured boundary.

⚠️ THE DEPLOY CADENCE IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT ON EVER SAMPLING THE TAIL, and it is worse than the earlier estimate: SIX processes in ~10 h (23:06 → 06:24 → 07:34 → 08:34 → 09:07), because ict-git-sync auto-deploys every merge to main and main is busy. Two of those six restarts were caused by THIS session's own merges. The only process that ever reached a large n was the one that ran through a quiet overnight window. So the per-process grade will read `within` on any active day regardless of the underlying distribution — read it beside intervals_measured, never alone.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR CLOSING THE ROW: criterion 1 is answered (tail, not trend) and criterion 2 is shipped and verified. What remains is NOT more spot reads — six processes of one-off snapshots is where this method runs out. A durable cross-process accumulator (the exposure_soak shape: append-only JSONL surviving restarts) is the only thing that would let anyone observe the tail on a normal day. Proposing it, not shipping it — it is a new writer on the live tick and wants its own review.

[sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Criterion 2 is shipped and verifiable in source: src/runtime/exit_loop_health.py measures max_interval_ms + intervals_measured and grades a four-state requirement_state against EXIT_EVAL_MAX_INTERVAL_SECONDS (lines 94-95,147-162,199-235), registered with collapsed-state-guard. Criterion 4 is answered (the 29.0s ceiling, split to BL-20260816-IB-QUEUE-TIMEOUT-EXCEEDS-EXIT-BUDGET, which I confirmed at src/exchange/ib_connector.py:113-131). Criterion 1's residual — keep sampling max_interval_ms across processes, always stating n and process start — is inherently live work. — needs live data: repeated /api/diag/log_file?name=exit_loop_health reads across several processes, each quoted with n and process_started_utc. Do not repeat the 'creeping toward 60s' framing — the row itself retracts it as a max-vs-mean and max-vs-n artefact.

DURABILITY FIXED (operator-directed). The residual on criterion 1 was 'more spot reads', which was the wrong answer: the per-process reset is not a sampling inconvenience, it is a BIASED MEASUREMENT. A max over a short window is systematically LOW, and the trader redeploys on every merge to main (six processes in ~10h on 2026-08-16, two of them caused by this session's own merges), so the in-memory grade reads most reassuring exactly when the system is busiest. The only reading that ever approached the requirement came from the one process that survived a quiet overnight window.

New `src/runtime/exit_interval_soak.py` appends one row per completed pass to runtime_logs/exit_interval_soak.jsonl (append-only, survives restarts), wired into exit_loop_health.record_pass OUTSIDE the state lock so a slow disk can never stall the exit loop, and registered on /api/diag/log_file?name=exit_interval_soak. summary.max_interval_ms is computed over the WHOLE FILE, not the returned page - truncating it would reintroduce the same windowing bias in the reader. The breach verdict is frozen at write time because the requirement is env-configurable and a reader recomputing it would silently re-grade history.

CORRECTION - IT IS FIVE OBSERVED PROCESSES, NOT SIX. Both earlier updates today said six; both were wrong, in two independent ways, and both errors are the same kind: counting a PROXY for a restart instead of an observed restart.

(a) The 09:26Z update's own table over-counts itself. It lists SIX ROWS but only FIVE distinct process_started_utc values - 2026-08-16T06:24:32Z appears twice (n=11 and n=38, two reads of ONE process as it accumulated). I counted reads as processes. The arithmetic was visible in the table I wrote.

(b) The 10:05Z update's 'six processes in ~10h' additionally inferred a ~09:55 restart from a merge to main. The data REFUTES it: sysrev-0816's read at 10:11Z reported bot_uptime_s 3895 (64.9 min), dating the then-running process to ~09:06:38 - i.e. still the 09:07:09 process. A merge does not promptly restart the trader; the deploy rides the ict-git-sync timer, so merge times are not restart times.

CORRECTED SERIES (five observed, counted from process_started_utc):
  23:06:29Z n=694 max 58940.8ms 98.2%
  06:24:32Z n=11 -> n=38 max 41543.5ms 69.2% (one process, two reads)
  07:34:25Z n=23 max 47449.6ms 79.1%
  08:34:15Z n=4 max 18691.4ms 31.2%
  09:07:09Z n=16 max 47196.3ms 78.7% (max_INTERVAL_ms, the new field)

NOTHING DOWNSTREAM CHANGES. Zero breaches still holds, the tail-not-trend finding on criterion 1 still holds (it never rested on the process count), and the durability argument is unaffected - it needs only that processes are short and frequent relative to the tail, which five in ~10h establishes as well as six. What DOES change is that a restart count must be measured from observed process_started_utc, never from merge times or from the number of reads taken. The count is corrected in the same breath in src/runtime/exit_interval_soak.py, src/runtime/exit_loop_health.py, src/web/api/routers/diag.py, tests/test_exit_interval_soak.py and CLAUDE.md (PR #9627).

DEPLOYED AND WRITING; DURABILITY STILL UNPROVEN. Relay #9665. /api/diag/version = 5e139dae (the #9627 merge commit), so the fix is live. /api/diag/log_file?name=exit_interval_soak returns present:true with 18 rows.

VERIFIED LIVE:
* interval_ms is null (NOT 0.0) on the process's first pass, with first_pass_of_process:true and over_requirement:null. The tri-state holds against a real gateway, so a restart gap cannot read as a real interval.
* 18 rows -> 17 intervals; the n/(n-1) relation reconciles.
* THE INSTRUMENTATION MEASURES WHAT IT CLAIMS, checked rather than assumed: against the period-targeting model interval = max(0, 30000 - prev_pass) + this_pass, 0 of 17 rows mismatch by more than 250ms. So the recorded value is genuinely sleep + pass -- the quantity the 60s requirement is written against.

NOT VERIFIED, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT: every row carries the same process_started_utc (2026-08-16T11:11:49.992412Z). ONE process. The claim the module exists to support -- that the max becomes a property of the DATA rather than of a process's lifetime -- requires summary.max_interval_ms spanning more than one process_started_utc, and that read does not exist yet. Row stays open.

READING (n=17 intervals, ~9 minutes, one process): max 48835.3ms = 81.4% of the requirement; mean 32234.7ms; ZERO breaches.

DO NOT READ THAT AS DEGRADATION. 48.8s at n=17 is a high draw for a nine-minute window (earlier daytime processes: 41.5s at n=38, 47.4s at n=23), but comparing maxima across different sample sizes is the exact error this row retracted earlier today -- and here the n is SMALLER while the max is LARGER, which is not a trend argument in either direction. It is consistent with the fat tail being drawn readily rather than growing, which points at bounding the tail (BL-20260816-IB-QUEUE-TIMEOUT-EXCEEDS-EXIT-BUDGET) rather than hunting a regression.

RE-MEASURED 2026-08-20 AND IT IS MATERIALLY WORSE THAN FILED. This row (and the CLAUDE.md row quoting it) records 58940.8 ms max at n=694, described as '1.1 s of margin' against the 60 s requirement. Measured now, two independent surfaces: (a) /api/diag/log_file?name=exit_loop_health at 2026-08-20T20:38:48Z, ONE process started 19:47:51Z -- passes 64, intervals_measured 63, max_interval_ms 78581.4 (78.6 s), requirement_state 'breached', interval_breaches 21 of 63 = 33.3%, last_breach_utc 20:38:48Z (the most recent pass), last_pass_ms 60862.3. state 'fresh' coexists with requirement_state 'breached', exactly as designed. (b) /api/diag/log_file?name=exit_interval_soak, the DURABLE half -- 398 measured intervals across 3 processes: max 83717.7 ms (83.7 s), mean 47319.4 ms, 114 of 398 breaching = 28.6%, p50 40.3 s, p90 71.2 s. THE P90 ALONE IS ABOVE THE REQUIREMENT. Because (b) spans three processes it is not the 'one long-lived process finally drew the tail' artifact the design warns about -- that caveat cuts the other way here: the breach is now the middle of the distribution, not its tail, and a MEAN of 47.3 s means the typical exit evaluation is already within striking distance of the bar. Escalating from a latency-budget note to a live requirement breach. POSSIBLY RELATED, stated as an observation and not a diagnosis: /api/bot/notifications concurrently carries 'monitor_blindness' and 'transient_market_data_unavailable: mes_trend_long_1d: no candle data returned for symbol=MES timeframe=1d'. The exit pass is documented as fetch-bound, and MES is also the leg whose venue stop diverges from its journal, so a monitor that cannot fetch is a plausible common factor for both. Not established.

[s1-q9kso 2026-08-22] RESOLVED alongside its two siblings by #10129 — see BL-20260816-IB-QUEUE-TIMEOUT-EXCEEDS-EXIT-BUDGET for the full population, the power note and the caveat that no post-deploy process has yet matched the 695-pass process the 89.35 s pre-deploy max came from. requirement_state now reads `within` with interval_breaches 0 at n=147.

items.title: The four-state prop `status_freshness` shipped in #9334 is NOT in collapsed-state-guard's CONTRACTS table, so the guard that exists to stop exactly this class of field from collapsing does not watch it
items.detail:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 during the session-end doc-freshness pass.

PR #9334 added a four-state field — `prop_reconcile._status_freshness` -> `ok` / `stale` / `absent` / `unchecked`, surfaced on `/api/bot/prop/status` and inside `rule_distance`, plus a fifth `error` on the envelope only. CLAUDE.md ("Collapsed states") states the rule plainly: *registering a contract in its `CONTRACTS` table is how a new three-state field becomes enforced.* It was not registered.

Verified by reading the guard, not inferred: `scripts/ci/check_collapsed_states.py` CONTRACTS currently holds exactly 7 keys — bybit_available.read_state, db_explorer.filter_state, db_explorer.order_state, exit_anchor.bar_close_at, netting_attribution.anchor_status, pairs_executor.leg_state, pairs_executor.open_state_read. `grep -c 'status_freshness' ` over that file returns 0.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING TEST. The guard passed on #9334 and will keep passing, because it only checks contracts that are registered. So the field is protected by nothing: a future edit could collapse `unchecked` into `ok` (the exact error the state exists to prevent — 'we did not look' is not 'fine'), or drop `absent`, and CI would stay green. An unregistered contract is indistinguishable from a field nobody thought about.

RESOLUTION: add `prop_status.status_freshness` to CONTRACTS naming producer `src/prop/prop_reconcile.py::_status_freshness` and consumers `src/web/api/routers/prop.py::get_status` + the dashboard/Android panels; assert all four states are emitted and branched on. Note the envelope-only `error` value is deliberately NOT one of the producer's four — the read failed before a snapshot was reached — so the contract should cover the four and the guard should not expect `error` from the producer.
items.resolution_criteria: `scripts/ci/check_collapsed_states.py` CONTRACTS contains prop_status.status_freshness; the guard fails if any of ok/stale/absent/unchecked is removed from the producer or left unbranched by a consumer; guard self-test covers the failure path.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Enumerated CONTRACTS in scripts/ci/check_collapsed_states.py by regex over its `"name":` keys — 8 entries: db_explorer.filter_state, db_explorer.order_state, exit_loop_health.requirement_state, exit_anchor.bar_close_at, pairs_executor.leg_state, pairs_executor.open_state_read, bybit_available.read_state, netting_attribution.anchor_status. No prop_status.status_freshness, so the four-state field shipped in #9334 is watched by nothing. — Tier-1 CI; registering the contract is exactly how CLAUDE.md says such a field becomes enforced.

CONFIRMED LIVE: I read collapsed-state-guard's full output this review — 19 contracts, and prop_status_freshness is NOT among them (the prop entry present is prop_rule_distance.balance_basis). So the four-state status_freshness shipped in #9334 is still unguarded, while /api/bot/prop/status returns status_freshness `ok` today on a 0.9 h-old snapshot. Registering it is cheap and is the same fix pattern as BL-20260813-MARGIN-BASIS-ABSENCE-IS-A-COLLAPSED-STATE and BL-20260814-VENUE-MAX-NONE-CANNOT-SAY-WE-COULD-NOT-LOOK.

items.source: The 2026-08-16 target-50 fleet stale re-sweep COMPLETED cleanly (19 legs, 252/252 cells measured, OOS landing 47-50 where derivable) and is UNUSABLE: its own SUMMARY.md reports `legacy (no TP cap)` on every one of the 19 legs. m20_fleet_exit_sweep.py:1463 declares `--tp-cap-pct` with default=0.0 and the launch omitted it.
items.title: [research] `--tp-cap-pct` defaults to 0.0, so forgetting the flag silently measures a book production does not run — it already wasted a full fleet re-sweep
items.description:
A re-sweep whose ENTIRE PURPOSE was to replace stale no-take-profit evidence was itself measured on a no-take-profit book. Its verdicts cannot re-grade the stale cells; they would substitute one staleness for another. The split-target half of the run worked (that is what makes it dangerous — the run looks successful and its headline numbers are real).

SAME DEFECT CLASS, THIRD INSTANCE. (1) m20_flip_replay_sweep called base_args() with five positionals so tp_cap_pct fell to its 0.0 default — every regime_flip_exit cell measured on a no-TP book (fixed in #9257). (2) Both M21 entry drivers had the identical positional bug across 227/227 cells (fixed on the M21 follow-up). (3) This one is not a code bug at all — it is a forgotten CLI flag. THE SHARED ROOT CAUSE IS THE DEFAULT: 0.0 makes the WRONG book the one you get by forgetting, and the run announces the choice only in a per-leg SUMMARY header that nobody diffs.

Note what did work: the header IS honest and per-leg, which is the only reason this was caught. The fix is not more prose, it is a default that fails safe.

FIX: make `--tp-cap-pct` default to live parity (0.099), or make it required so the caller must state the geometry. Tier-1 mechanically, but it re-points what a bare invocation MEANS for every future run, so it wants an explicit decision rather than a silent flip — flagged to the operator 2026-08-16. The M21 drivers were given the 0.099 default in the same cycle, where there was no prior default to re-point.
items.trigger_condition: A sweep SUMMARY reports `legacy (no TP cap)` for a leg on a TP-capped family (donchian/pullback/fade/squeeze), or a verdict is quoted from such a run.
items.resolution_criteria: (1) `--tp-cap-pct` on m20_fleet_exit_sweep either defaults to 0.099 or has no default and errors when omitted; (2) a test asserts that default so it cannot drift back; (3) the 2026-08-16 legacy-geometry run is either re-run at live parity or explicitly marked unusable wherever it is referenced, so no cell is re-graded from it.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: scripts/research/m20_fleet_exit_sweep.py:1607 still declares `--tp-cap-pct` with `default=0.0`, so a bare invocation still measures the legacy no-take-profit book — while its own siblings now default to live parity (m21_entry_sweep.py:104 and m21_entry_head_round.py:96 both default=0.099). No test pins the default either. — Proposed (operator sign-off because it re-points what every bare invocation MEANS): change m20_fleet_exit_sweep's `--tp-cap-pct` default to 0.099 (matching the m21/flip siblings) or make it required so the caller must state the geometry, add a test pinning it, and mark the 2026-08-16 legacy-geometry fleet run unusable wherever it is referenced so no cell is re-graded from it.

items.resolution_note: RESOLVED 2026-08-16 by the operator's Tier-3 default flip (in-conversation). `--tp-cap-pct` now defaults to LIVE_TP_CAP_PCT=0.099 and `--split-target-oos` to DEFAULT_SPLIT_TARGET_OOS=50, separated from the MIN_OOS_TRADES=25 floor it used to equal. Passing `--tp-cap-pct 0` is now the explicit opt-out and is REQUIRED to reproduce any verdict recorded before 2026-08-10. The default was the whole finding, so flipping it closes this row outright.

items.source: Filed issue #9559 with `trainer-vm-heavy-request` following the VM-lane protocol; it sat silent. Enumerated every issues-triggered workflow's label filter: trainer-vm-diag consumes `trainer-vm-diag-request`, trainer-offload-train consumes `trainer-offload-train-request`, research-exit-head-replay-trainer consumes `exit-head-replay-request`. Nothing consumes `trainer-vm-heavy-request`.
items.title: [tooling] `trainer-vm-heavy-request` is declared AND hook-enforced but no workflow triggers on it — a heavy job filed per the VM-lane protocol never runs and never fails
items.description:
The label is created by bootstrap-labels.yml:335 and ENFORCED by .claude/hooks/vm_lane_guard.sh, which denies an issue_write carrying it unless the session holds a fresh VM-lane claim marker. So a session that follows session-coordination SKILL.md correctly — claim the lane, file with the heavy label — gets an open issue that is never picked up.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY DEAD PATH: the enforcement layer in front of it makes it look load-bearing, and there is NO failure comment. The skill's own safeguard ('never wait indefinitely on a dispatched run; treat a failure/cancelled comment as terminal') cannot fire, because silence is indistinguishable from queued. Same shape as the written-and-never-read guard findings from the same morning.

WORKAROUND in use: file heavy jobs under `trainer-vm-diag-request` and keep the VM-lane claim on the board; `nohup ... &` a long command so the relay job returns instead of holding a runner.
items.trigger_condition: An issue labelled `trainer-vm-heavy-request` receives no workflow comment within the relay's normal turnaround.
items.resolution_criteria: (1) `trainer-vm-heavy-request` appears in the label filter of a workflow that actually runs it (adding it to trainer-vm-diag.yml's `contains(...)` condition is sufficient — the relay already does what a heavy job needs); (2) a heavy-labelled issue is dispatched end-to-end and comments back; (3) EITHER that, or the label and its hook-enforcement are removed together and the skill text updated, so the protocol never again names a path with no consumer.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Confirmed: `grep -rn 'trainer-vm-heavy-request' .github/workflows/*.yml .claude/hooks/*.sh` returns only bootstrap-labels.yml:335 (which CREATES the label) and .claude/hooks/vm_lane_guard.sh:14,45,60 (which ENFORCES a VM-lane claim before an issue may carry it). No workflow's label filter contains it, so a correctly-filed heavy job opens an issue nothing picks up and nothing fails. — Tier-1 tooling. Worse than an ordinary dead path because the hook enforcement in front of it makes it read as load-bearing and silence is indistinguishable from queued.

notes.note: [FIXED 2026-08-16, operator-directed] trainer-vm-diag.yml's job condition now fires on trainer-vm-heavy-request as well as trainer-vm-diag-request (resolution option (a) of this row's own criteria). The VM-lane FIFO is a BOARD convention, not a workflow feature, so the two labels need no behavioural difference — the heavy one exists to trip the vm_lane_guard claim check, and it must still RUN. Verified: yaml parses and the condition contains both labels. STILL OPEN, deliberately, is the GENERAL half this row also names: a labelled issue that no workflow picks up is still indistinguishable from one that succeeded. That needs a sweep that comments on any relay-labelled issue with no run attached after N minutes -- filed separately rather than marked done here.

items.resolution_note: RESOLVED 2026-08-16 by PR #9704, merged to main as 84a511ae. Verified ON MAIN after the merge, not inferred from it: trainer-vm-diag.yml's job condition parses with both 'trainer-vm-diag-request' and 'trainer-vm-heavy-request'; vm-diag-snapshot.yml carries the slashless-prefix strip in BOTH resolvers (the shell workflow_dispatch path AND the Python resolve_one on the issues path, which is the one sessions actually use) plus a doubled-prefix backstop at 2 sites. The backstop was falsified rather than assumed: deleting the strip made it raise "doubled upstream prefix: resolved '/api/diag/api/diag/status' from input 'api/diag/status'", proving the two layers are independent. NOTE the duplicate pair: this gap was filed twice by two different sessions and fixed zero times until an operator directive overruled filing it a third time.

items.source: Swept docs/research/exit-refinement-coverage.json while working the exit_head_ml column. `lifetime_trades` is recorded on 11 of 416 cells — and those 11 are exactly the exit_head_ml cells the roll-up grades arithmetically.
items.title: [research] 7 blocked matrix cells name a TRADE-COUNT reason while recording no trade count — the claim cannot be checked from the artifact that makes it
items.description:
MEASURED 2026-08-16. Of 18 blocked cells whose status names a count (`insufficient_lifetime_trades` / `insufficient_base` / `insufficient_oos_base_at_derived_split`), 11 record `lifetime_trades` and **7 do not**:
  spy_trend_long_1d/vol_trail and qld_trend_long_1d/vol_trail literally read `blocked:insufficient_lifetime_trades` with `lifetime_trades: None`;
  iwm_/splg_trend_long_1d/vol_trail read `insufficient_oos_base_at_derived_split`;
  mes_trend_long_1d/{giveback_stop,vol_trail} and mhg_pullback_1d/giveback_stop read `insufficient_base`.

WHAT MAKES IT A DEFECT RATHER THAN AN OMISSION: the SAME legs carry the number on their exit_head_ml cell (spy 48, qld 31), so the value existed and simply was not stamped on the sibling that cites it. The roll-up can therefore say of exit_head_ml '11 of 11 cannot form a SINGLE fold — the block is arithmetic, not data availability', per leg and checkable, while vol_trail blocks making the SAME KIND of claim cannot be checked at all. A reader cannot distinguish 'we measured too few trades' from 'we asserted too few trades'.

The claims are probably TRUE (spy 48 and qld 31 are consistent with an insufficiency verdict) — that is not the point. This is the unasserted-denominator shape at cell level: a blocked cell is a verdict, and a verdict that names a quantity should carry it. It also caps what the roll-up can ever automate — it can only grade blocks it can read a count for, which today is 11 cells.

RELATED, and deliberately NOT folded in: ict_scalp_mgc_15m/exit_head_ml is `blocked:native-history-thin` with no count, which is CORRECT — that block is about a data SOURCE (IBKR serves ~1yr of MGC 15m, flat-bar contaminated; the Dukascopy spot-XAU proxy is rejected for head training per the mgc_pullback_1d precedent), not about trade volume. A source-shaped block should not be made to carry a count.
items.trigger_condition: A matrix cell's status names a count-based block reason while its `lifetime_trades` (or the relevant base/OOS count) is absent.
items.resolution_criteria: (1) Every blocked cell whose reason names a count records that count in the cell; (2) the writer that stamps a count-based block reason stamps the count in the same place, so the two cannot diverge; (3) a check fails when a count-naming block reason appears without its number — the 7 known cells are either filled in or re-typed to a non-count reason. Source-shaped blocks (e.g. native-history-thin) are explicitly exempt and must stay exempt.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Re-measured over docs/research/exit-refinement-coverage.json: 18 cells carry a count-naming block reason and exactly 7 have `lifetime_trades: None` — mes_trend_long_1d/{giveback_stop,vol_trail}, mhg_pullback_1d/giveback_stop, spy_ and qld_trend_long_1d/vol_trail (insufficient_lifetime_trades), iwm_ and splg_trend_long_1d/vol_trail (insufficient_oos_base_at_derived_split). Same 7 the row names. — The values exist on the same legs' exit_head_ml cells (spy 48, qld 31), so the cheap half is stamping them; the durable half is the writer stamping the count wherever it writes a count-naming reason, plus a check.
Re-validated: 7 cells naming a trade-count reason while recording no trade count — an unverifiable claim, the stated-population rule applied to the matrix.

items.tier: 2 (it bounds a live fetch the exit loop makes; changing it is not a docs edit)
items.title: A single IB fetch queue timeout consumes 48% of the 60s exit-evaluation budget, and the two numbers were set in different sessions with no reference to each other
items.detail:
_IB_FETCH_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_S (src/exchange/ib_connector.py:113) is 29.0s, derived as
IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S * 3.0 + 5.0 with IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S unset live (get-env #9570)
so the 8.0 default applies. _IB_USAGE_LOCK_WAIT_S is likewise 24.0s (*3.0).

BASIS FOR THE FIGURES BELOW, since two different kinds of number appear here.
The percentages are ARITHMETIC on two constants (29.0 / 60.0), not a sample: they
state what one timeout WOULD cost, and hold whenever it fires. The observations they
are set against are: max pass 58940.8ms over n=694 passes on the process started
2026-08-15T23:06:29Z, and max pass 40872.5ms over n=11 on the process started
2026-08-16T06:24:32Z. How OFTEN the timeout fires is NOT measured - see criterion 1;
that missing denominator is the reason this row proposes no value.

The exit loop calls get_ohlcv. So a SINGLE queue timeout inside one exit pass costs
48.3% of the operator's 60s max-interval requirement; two cost 96.7%; three exceed it
outright at 87s. The worst pass of those n=694, 58940.8ms, is 2 x 29000 + 941.

NEITHER CONSTANT IS WRONG ON ITS OWN TERMS. 29.0s was sized to outlast a queued-but-
healthy fetch so a real one is never discarded as a failure - correct in isolation,
and its comment says exactly that. The 60s requirement was set for the M20 decouple.
The defect is at the SEAM: the pin (#9240) put the exit loop and the main tick on ONE
serialised IB thread, which is what makes a 29s queue wait reachable from inside an
exit pass at all, and no session checked the fetch-path bound against the exit-path
requirement. Same shape as the tick-cost class - each component individually bounded
and documented as cheap, the SUM never watched.

NOT PROPOSING A VALUE. Lowering 29.0s trades a longer exit interval for more
degraded (None) fetches, and a None fetch means the monitor evaluates that symbol on
no candles - which is the MONITOR BLIND condition, not a cheaper outcome. Choosing
between them needs the distribution of how often the timeout actually fires, which is
not currently measured anywhere: the warning is logged but never counted, and the
journalctl relay truncates too aggressively to count it after the fact.

--- 2026-08-21T17:45Z, session wave0-8g7443: A ROUTE THAT NEEDS NO VALUE FOR THIS CONSTANT ---

This row correctly declines to propose a value, because lowering 29.0s buys degraded (None)
fetches and a None fetch is the MONITOR BLIND condition. Wave 0.1 found a way to attack the
QUEUE DEPTH instead of the timeout, which needs no such trade.

Every IB candle fetch is an uncacheable venue round trip: _client_cache_key
(src/runtime/market_data.py:48) excludes interactive_brokers from the connector memo, so a
fresh IBMarketData is built per request and the candle cache - keyed on a per-object token -
can never hit. Measured: off-loop fetch.15m ran 281 fetches in 281 passes for ONE open IB
package (1.000/pass, zero hits). All of those submissions go to _IB_FETCH_EXECUTOR, the
max_workers=1 pool (src/exchange/ib_connector.py:103) shared by the tick thread and the exit
thread - which is what makes a 29s queue wait reachable from inside an exit pass at all.

Memoizing the IB connector (proposal: docs/research/exit-eval-fetch-attribution-2026-08-21.md)
would cut off-loop IB submissions from ~2/pass toward ~0.6/pass and on-loop from ~4/tick
toward ~1/tick. Fewer submissions is strictly less queue depth. That is a MECHANISM, not a
measurement - this row's criterion 1 (how often the timeout actually fires) is still
unmeasured, and still cannot be measured from the surfaces that exist today,
because the fetch instrument has no venue axis (BL-20260821-FETCH-COST-HAS-NO-VENUE-AXIS).
checked: src/runtime/tick_cost.py — read the emitter directly: it records fetches under
fetch.<timeframe> and fetchby.<phase> and nowhere keys on venue or symbol, so no
aggregation of its output can separate an IB fetch from an Alpaca one. This is a claim
about ONE instrument, not about the world: a venue cut is cheap to add (3 names against
_MAX_HOOK_NAMES=64, live chain measured at 27), which is exactly what that row proposes.

ON THE ~26.6s CEILING: every frame that includes an IB symbol shows a max of 26.0-26.8s
(fetch.1d 26795.0ms, fetch.15m 26514.6ms, fetch.1h 26665.3ms, fetch.5m 26047.8ms) while
fetch.2h (676.9ms) and fetch.4h (323.3ms) - the two frames with no IB leg - do not. That is
CONSISTENT WITH the 29.0s bound and is NOT confirmation: 2h and 4h have far lower n (150 and
82 on-loop) and may simply have missed the stall windows. Recorded as consistent-with rather
than promoted to a cause.
items.resolution_criteria:
BASIS: the percentages here are ARITHMETIC on two constants (29.0 / 60.0), not a
sample - they state what one timeout WOULD cost whenever it fires. The observations
they are set against are max pass 58940.8ms over n=694 passes (process started
2026-08-15T23:06:29Z) and max pass 40872.5ms over n=11 (process started
2026-08-16T06:24:32Z). How OFTEN it fires is UNMEASURED, which is criterion 1 and the
reason this row proposes no value.

1. COUNT IT FIRST. Add a counter for the _IB_FETCH_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_S and
_IB_USAGE_LOCK_WAIT_S paths (both currently log-only) so the firing RATE is a number
rather than an inference from a max. Tier-1, and it is the prerequisite for the rest.
2. Only then decide whether 29.0s belongs inside a 60s budget, and state explicitly
what the alternative costs in degraded fetches - do not optimise the interval into a
MONITOR BLIND.
3. Consider decoupling the derivation: the queue timeout is currently a function of
IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S, so tuning the per-request cap silently moves the exit budget too.

updates.note: [sysrev-0816 2026-08-16] re-validated this run: Both constants are as filed and neither is counted: src/exchange/ib_connector.py:113-117 derives `_IB_FETCH_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_S` as IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S*3.0+5.0 (29.0s at the unset 8.0 default) and :127-131 derives `_IB_USAGE_LOCK_WAIT_S` as *3.0 (24.0s); the two use sites (:273 future.result(timeout=…) and :161/:315 lock.acquire) are log-only — there is no counter or tick_cost hook on either path, so the firing RATE is still unmeasured. — Criterion 1 (add the counters) is the prerequisite and it sits in the live IB fetch path (Tier-2 in this row's own framing), so it is outside what I may edit here. Until the rate is a number, no value change should be proposed.

[s1-q9kso 2026-08-22, workplan item 1.0] CRITERION 1 IS NOW MEASURED, AND THIS ROW'S PREMISE IS REFUTED. The queue timeout was never observed firing. `timed out waiting for the pinned IB thread` (the _IB_FETCH_QUEUE_TIMEOUT_S log line) and `could not acquire the IB client's usage lock` (the _IB_USAGE_LOCK_WAIT_S line) each appear ZERO times in every journal window sampled: four disjoint windows spanning 2026-08-22T01:30Z-07:40Z totalling 2226s, plus 07:55Z-08:09Z. The firing rate this row could not put a number on is 0, so the 48.3%/96.7%/87s arithmetic — correct as arithmetic — describes a cost that is not being paid, and 29.0s must NOT be lowered on the strength of it (doing so would have traded real fetches for MONITOR BLIND to fix nothing, which is precisely what criterion 2 warned against). THE REAL CAUSE IS `IBClient._probe_liveness`. It runs inside connect(), which _get_ohlcv_pinned calls on every fetch — cached handle included. Measured over the same four windows: n=75 attempt-1 timeouts / 2226s = 2.02/min (within-window 1.50-2.32/min), each costing IB_PROBE_TIMEOUT_S 5.0s + IB_PROBE_RETRY_GAP_S 1.5s = 6.5s, i.e. 488s of blocking in 2226s = 21.9% of wall clock; `liveness probe timed out twice` (the condemning branch) fired ZERO times in that population. Isolated inside one breaching exit pass by journal gaps (pass ending 07:37:07Z, 51.4s): trend_donchian_eth_4h 07:36:23.422 -> mes_trend_long_1d 07:36:43.665 = 20.24s, -> mhg_pullback_1d 07:37:03.892 = 20.23s; every other leg in that pass took ~0.4s. Two IB fetches = 40.5s of a 51.4s pass. STATE THE POPULATION: that is the TIMEOUT branch. The probe's `except` branch DID condemn correctly at 08:06:15Z on a genuine `ConnectionError: Socket disconnect` (gateway peer-closed, all three clients tripped) — real detection, and untouched by the fix, because a closed socket fails _is_connected and forces a FRESH connect, which always probes. FIX SHIPPED: IB_PROBE_CACHE_S (default 60s) trusts a SUCCESSFUL probe for a window on a still-connected cached handle. It can only ever skip a repeat of a check that already passed, never add one, so the probe count is monotonically non-increasing. Falsified by tests/test_ib_probe_cache.py (8 failed / 1 passed pre-fix, 9 passed post-fix) plus a behavioural control loading both file versions in one process: 10 connect() calls on one cached live handle run 10 probes pre-fix and 1 post-fix. Criterion 3 (the derivation coupling queue timeout to IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S) is UNCHANGED and still stands as a separate concern.

[s1-q9kso 2026-08-22] RESOLVED — shipped (#10129, squash 9c9235f) and LIVE-CONTROLLED. Deployed 9c9235f6, confirmed by ANCESTRY (git merge-base --is-ancestor), not by a SHA string. POST-DEPLOY, stated population: (a) probe rate — 0 attempt-1 timeouts over 1395 s across three consecutive windows 08:35-08:59Z, against a pre-deploy 75/2226 s = 2.02/min, so ~47 were expected; the IDENTICAL grep returned 75 pre-deploy, so this is a measured absence, not a broken probe. (b) exit_interval_soak, one process 08:34:39-09:42Z, n=147 intervals: max_interval_ms 89350.9 -> 39644.4 (-55.6%), p99 67613.8 -> 36033.1, breaches 18/991 (1.82%) -> 0/147 (0%), max pass_ms 69140.8 -> 15445.3 (-77.7%), mean pass 5079.1 -> 2111.1. (c) off-loop fetchvenue.interactive_brokers mean 1336.4 ms (n=48) -> 65.6 ms (n=423). POWER, STATED HONESTLY BECAUSE THE HEADLINE COMPARISON IS THE WEAK ONE: the breach-count test alone is underpowered at this n — 2.67 expected, P(0)=0.069. The powered test is passes>30 s, which is also the mechanistically correct threshold given interval = max(0, 30000 - pass_prev) + pass_curr: 31/1000 = 3.10% pre-deploy predicts 4.59 in 148 post-deploy passes, 0 observed, P(0)=0.010. The probe-rate test is stronger still. A reader should not quote the max-vs-max comparison alone. REMAINING/UNCHANGED: criterion 3 of this row (the queue timeout is derived from IB_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S, so tuning the per-request cap silently moves the exit budget) is UNTOUCHED and still stands as a separate concern. The 29.0 s constant was NOT changed — correctly, since it never fires.
