items.title: A session that pip-installs a dependency conftest deliberately STUBS turns local-green into CI-red, and the divergence is invisible until CI says so
items.detail: FILED BY MI-92 from its own CI failure, as an out-of-scope observation. requirements-test.txt does NOT install python-telegram-bot -- tests/conftest.py stubs `telegram` (and .ext/.error/.constants) with a bare MagicMock, and the file says so explicitly. A session working on src/bot/ cannot run the suite at all without SOME telegram module, so the natural move is `pip install python-telegram-bot`, which is what this session did. From that moment the local environment DIVERGES FROM CI IN THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION: assertions that touch the real library's behaviour pass locally and fail in CI. MEASURED HERE: three new tests asserting MenuButtonCommands().type == 'commands' and MenuButtonWebApp(...).type == 'web_app' passed locally and took pytest-run RED on PR #10916 head 5170fd4d, while guards / pytest-collect / repo-inventory all went green -- so the green checks gave no hint. Reproduced deliberately rather than reasoned about: uninstalling python-telegram-bot recreated the CI condition exactly, the pushed state then failed precisely those three tests, and the fix took it to 217 passed / 4 skipped under the same stub. NOTE the bare-MagicMock stub makes `from telegram import AnythingAtAll` SUCCEED, so the failure never surfaces as an ImportError at collection -- it surfaces only as an assertion on a Mock, deep in a test, which is why it reads as a logic bug rather than an environment one. ⚠️ THIS IS THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION TO BL-20260826-SANDBOX-FULL-SUITE-CARRIES-32-FAILURES-CI-DOES-NOT-AND-5-ARE-ORDER-DEPENDENT (local carries failures CI lacks, so the local run is PESSIMISTIC and merely noisy). This one is OPTIMISTIC: the local run is cleaner than CI, which is the direction that ships. The two must not be folded together.
items.resolution_criteria: Either (a) a test-side convention makes this class unreachable -- e.g. a conftest assertion that fails loudly when a module listed in its stub set is importable for real, so a session with the library installed is TOLD its environment differs rather than discovering it from CI; or (b) requirements-test.txt / the contributing notes state the trap at the point of use, i.e. where a session decides to install the library. NOT sufficient: this backlog row alone -- it is the same 'documented in a place nobody reads mid-task' shape that this repo has already paid for twice (BL-20260720-GH-ACTIONS-PUSH-EVENTS-DEAD -> BL-20260830-ZERO-CHECK-RUNS-READ-AS-CI-NOT-STARTED-NOT-AS-MERGE-CONFLICT). NOT sufficient either: telling sessions not to install it, since the suite cannot be run on src/bot/ without something in that slot.

items.title: OPEN-ITEMS.json — the register with the HIGHEST row contention — has no append helper, and backlog_append refuses it
items.detail: MEASURED 2026-09-03 on main @855397f6. `scripts/ops/backlog_append.py::append_row` raises FormatNotReproducible on docs/claude/OPEN-ITEMS.json: none of its five candidate serialisations reproduces the file byte-for-byte. The file indents array ELEMENTS one level shallower than json.dumps does at any indent setting, so the closest candidates (indent=2 and indent=1, ensure_ascii=False) each differ on 236 of 1,065 lines. The refusal is CORRECT — it is the helper working as designed, and a naive round-trip would rewrite 2,082 lines and re-attribute all 50 pre-existing rows to whoever appended. But the consequence is that the ONE register a session cannot safely append to with any tool is also the one MI-76 measured as having the HIGHEST row contention: 23 of 65 adjacent commit pairs (35%) row-contested, versus 9% for health-review-backlog. Every append to it today is a hand edit. POPULATION: the 5 registers named in .gitattributes; OPEN-ITEMS.json is the only one append_row cannot write. Not fixed here because MI-94's scope is the id-uniqueness guard and the session-key check; writing a serialiser for this file is a separate, riskier change that must round-trip byte-for-byte before it writes anything.
items.resolution_criteria: Either (a) `backlog_append.append_row` writes docs/claude/OPEN-ITEMS.json with `--check-round-trip`-style byte-identical proof on the untouched file, or (b) OPEN-ITEMS.json is re-serialised ONCE to a shape append_row already reproduces, in a PR whose diff is that reformat ALONE and nothing else. Verified by appending a probe row and observing a diff of <15 lines, then deleting it.

items.title: pr-landing-guard R11 red-locks the entire automation PR lane, because a generating workflow cannot know to write a landing declaration
items.summary: MEASURED on PR #10914 (guards job 100580495407, 2026-09-03T08:35:45Z): PASS 45 / FAIL 1 / SKIP 37, and the single failure is `R11 no landing declaration at .github/pr-landing/automation-work-digest-33730997742-1.json`. scripts/ci/check_pr_landing.py contains ZERO occurrences of 'automation', 'exempt', 'bot[' or any equivalent (grep, whole file) -- it has no concept of a machine-authored PR. R11 asks whether the branch was cut from a main that already carried the guard; every automation branch cut after MI-88 landed this morning answers yes and fails, permanently, because the GENERATING WORKFLOW does not write a declaration and cannot be told to by the branch it creates. POPULATION at 09:10Z: 8 open automation PRs -- #10919 (strategy-reviews), #10914/#10908/#10902 (work-digest x3), #10913/#10907/#10901 (reconcile-open-prs x3), #10398 (econ-calendar, cut 08-29 and therefore PRE-guard, a control that should NOT fail this way). The duplicates are the tell: each family re-fires on its cadence and stacks, because nothing can merge. TWO CONSEQUENCES THAT ARE NOT COSMETIC: (1) reconcile-open-prs keeps docs/claude/work/OPEN-PRS.json honest, and that file is the OPEN-PR half of the manager handoff contract -- it now goes stale by construction while the register that tracks PR staleness is itself the thing that cannot land; (2) work-digest is the operator's digest carrier, which OI-20260902-DIGEST-MOVED-OFF-A-CRON-THAT-DOES-NOT-FIRE is actively watching -- its clause (1) asks for a push-triggered run whose receipt appears ON MAIN, and a receipt PR that can never merge cannot satisfy it. So this defect can make an open monitoring row read as an unproven carrier when the real cause is a guard downstream of it.
items.evidence: guards job 100580495407 (PR #10914): 'pr-landing-guard FAILED (state=undeclared)' + 'R11 no landing declaration at .github/pr-landing/automation-work-digest-33730997742-1.json'. grep -n 'automation|EXEMPT|exempt|dependabot|bot\[' scripts/ci/check_pr_landing.py returns nothing. list_pull_requests(state=open) at 2026-09-03T09:10Z shows the 8 rows above.
items.resolution_criteria: An automation PR is OBSERVED merging green -- not the guard passing in a self-test, and not a hand-written declaration dropped onto one branch. The two candidate fixes are NOT equivalent and the choice must be recorded: (a) make each generating workflow WRITE its own .github/pr-landing/<slug>.json (tier 1, landing self) as part of the commit it already makes -- keeps the invariant that no PR lands undeclared, and is the recommended route; or (b) exempt automation/** in the guard -- cheaper, and it creates an UNGUARDED LANE on the guard's first day, which is the failure this repo names as 'a guard cheaper to lie to than to satisfy is worse than no guard'. If (b) is chosen anyway, the exemption must be NARROW (a named branch-prefix allowlist, never a bot-author test) and must be recorded as a deliberate decision rather than a fix. ALSO REQUIRED EITHER WAY: the stacked duplicates must be drained, and #10398 checked separately -- it was cut 2026-08-29, BEFORE the guard, so if it fails R11 too then the 'branch could have known' test is not doing what its docstring claims and that is a SECOND, worse finding.
items.notes: SELF-INFLICTED, SAME DAY. The guard shipped this morning as MI-88 (the landing route) and this is its first contact with the machine-authored population, which nobody enumerated before landing it. Filed by the manager session as a routing disposition, not fixed here.

items.title: pr-opener.yml opens EVERY PR as a draft: `jq -r '.draft // true'` returns true for `false`, so `draft:false` is unreachable — and .github/pr-landing/README.md asserts the opposite
items.detail: MEASURED 2026-09-03. `.github/workflows/pr-opener.yml:123` reads `[ "$(jq -r '.draft // true' "$req")" = "true" ] && draft_flag="--draft"`. jq's `//` is the ALTERNATIVE operator and treats BOTH `null` AND `false` as empty, so `.draft // true` evaluates to `true` for every possible input. Tested directly, all 4 cases of the input domain: draft=true -> true; draft=false -> true; draft=null -> true; draft absent -> true. 4 of 4 yield `--draft`. The correct form is `jq -r 'if has("draft") then .draft else true end'`, verified to return false for draft=false and true for draft=true. LIVE PROOF: PR #10910 was opened through this relay from automation/pr-requests/mi94-register-id-uniqueness-open.json carrying `"draft": false`, and GitHub reports `draft: true`. THIS IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT COSMETIC: `claude-pr-automerge` refuses to arm auto-merge against a draft BY DESIGN (a correct safety property that must not be weakened), so every PR opened via this relay is structurally unable to self-land, however green it goes and however correctly it declares `landing: "self"`. That is precisely the failure `.github/pr-landing/` was built on 2026-09-03 to end. WARNING, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT NEEDS A HUMAN: `.github/pr-landing/README.md` currently states -- 'Three of those PR bodies blamed pr-opener.yml for "creating every PR as a draft regardless of draft:false". That is false and should not be repeated. pr-opener.yml honours draft:false; true is only the default, and those sessions' request files asked for "draft": true.' The first half of that correction is itself WRONG on the measurement above: the relay does NOT honour draft:false and cannot. Those three sessions may have mis-stated the CAUSE while reporting a real SYMPTOM, and the standing correction now instructs future sessions not to report the true observation. A doc that forbids repeating a true finding is worse than a silent bug. Whether those specific three request files asked for `true` is a separate claim this row does not adjudicate -- it was not re-read. POPULATION: 1 workflow file, 1 line; the jq behaviour was tested over the complete 4-case input domain; 1 live PR (#10910) confirms end to end. NOT FIXED HERE because MI-94's scope is register storage and the id-uniqueness guard, and because pr-landing-guard R12 exists precisely to stop a PR that already edits landing machinery from also editing the landing route it would then be merged by.
items.resolution_criteria: `.github/workflows/pr-opener.yml` uses a form that distinguishes an absent key from an explicit `false` (e.g. `jq -r 'if has("draft") then .draft else true end'`), AND a request file carrying `"draft": false` is observed opening a NON-draft PR -- read `draft` off the GitHub API on that PR, never off the workflow file or the run log. Separately and independently: the paragraph in .github/pr-landing/README.md that calls the draft-false claim 'false and should not be repeated' is corrected, so the doc no longer instructs sessions to suppress a true observation. Both halves are needed; fixing the code while leaving the doc standing leaves the next session told not to look.

items.summary: check_pr_landing.py's LANDING_MACHINERY list (the set R8 verifies a `changes_landing_machinery` hold against, and that R12 uses to refuse self-landing) names 7 paths and does NOT include scripts/ci/run_guards.py or scripts/ci/guard_selftests.py. Found 2026-09-03 while declaring MI-95's landing: a PR that registers a new guard in run_guards.py was REFUSED the `changes_landing_machinery` hold reason, correctly by the list as written. But run_guards.py is invoked by .github/workflows/guards.yml, which is a required check: a malformed entry there breaks the gate that decides whether ANYTHING merges. By any functional definition that is landing machinery. POPULATION: read from LANDING_MACHINERY in scripts/ci/check_pr_landing.py at commit b596d4bc -- 7 entries, enumerated, neither of these among them.
items.why_it_matters: Two directions, and both are live. (1) A guard-registration PR that genuinely wants a human read cannot say so in the closed vocabulary, so it either self-lands or reaches for a token that is not true -- and the vocabulary exists precisely to stop the second. (2) R12 exists so that a change to the landing route cannot approve itself; a PR that edits the guard RUNNER can today self-land while a PR that edits check_pr_landing.py cannot, and the runner is the thing that decides whether the check runs at all.
items.resolution_criteria: EITHER scripts/ci/run_guards.py (and guard_selftests.py) are added to LANDING_MACHINERY, with check_pr_landing.py's own self-test extended to prove R8 verifies the new entries and R12 refuses a self-land that touches them; OR the omission is argued as DELIBERATE in the module docstring, in the same explicit way `.github/pr-automerge-requests/**` is already argued as excluded, naming why the runner is different from the route. NOT resolved by adding the paths silently: the docstring already reasons at length about which paths belong and why, and an unexplained addition would decay to a list nobody can audit. ⚠️ Widening the list hands the `changes_landing_machinery` excuse to every guard PR -- weigh that against the pr-automerge-requests precedent, where an excuse every branch could satisfy was judged to excuse nothing.

items.summary: MEASURED 2026-09-03 from sub-session session_017DxuurbMW5ex5Q1f7xATqW, while verifying the operator's R13 ruling (a manager-constraining PR needs an operator GitHub approving review) rather than assuming it: (a) `get_me` returns `login: benbaichmankass, id: 119055177` -- the REPO OWNER's own account, NOT a bot identity. A session does not merely act for the owner, it authenticates AS the owner, so any review it could submit would carry the owner's login. (b) `pull_request_review_write` (method create, pending, no event) on #10918 returns `Resource not accessible by integration`. So THIS session cannot write reviews -- but the barrier is a TOKEN PERMISSION SCOPE, not an identity boundary. POPULATION: 3 distinct calls on this session's credential -- create_pull_request 403, update_pull_request(draft:false) 403, pull_request_review_write 403. All three are GitHub `pull_requests: write`.
items.why_it_matters: The R13 ruling's stated basis is that a session 'cannot forge it, cannot write it into the repo, and does not hold the credential'. The third clause is FALSE as measured, and the first two hold only while the scope stays narrow. Two consequences, both live. (1) `PATCH /pulls/:n` (un-draft) and `POST /pulls/:n/reviews` (approve) are the SAME `pull_requests: write` scope -- so granting sessions the un-draft ability they keep asking for (needed today on #10918, which a sub-session cannot mark ready) would make owner approvals forgeable AT THE SAME INSTANT, silently, with R13 still reading green. The remedy for one problem disarms the guard for the other. (2) The manager session demonstrably holds a WIDER scope than a sub-session -- it merges PRs, which a sub-session cannot. Whether that wider scope already includes review-write is UNMEASURED and is the load-bearing question: if the manager can approve as `benbaichmankass`, then R13 is satisfiable by the constrained party and the mechanism is theatre. ⚠️ This is 'we did not look', not 'it is fine' -- no session can test another session's credential.
items.resolution_criteria: FIRST, the unmeasured half: the lease-holding manager session runs `pull_request_review_write` (method create, NO event, pending) against any open PR and reports the result verbatim, then deletes the pending review. A 403 means the scope is narrow for the manager too and R13 can be built on it WITH the caveat documented; a success means R13 must NOT be built on GitHub review approval at all, because the constrained party can satisfy it. THEN, whichever way it goes: R13 may only be shipped with its actual basis stated (a permission scope, revocable and widenable) rather than the false one (an identity boundary), plus a tripwire that FAILS if a session's credential ever gains review-write -- a CI check cannot detect this (CI runs a different token), so it belongs in `scripts/ops/manager_preflight.py` or the session-start path. ⚠️ NOT resolved by shipping R13 and describing it as independent: a false independence claim is worse than the honest current state, which is the operator's and the manager's own stated bar. THE ONLY TRUE FIXES need an action outside the repo: sessions authenticating as a GitHub App or a distinct machine account rather than as the owner, so that 'approved by the owner' becomes a signal no session can produce regardless of scope.

items.summary: MEASURED 2026-09-03 while verifying (not adopting) the proposed R13 mechanism -- 'the approval record is written by the decision round-trip, so a guard can require it was committed by that path and carries the answering Telegram user id'. THE TELEGRAM USER ID IS NOT IN THE RECORD AS A TRUSTWORTHY FACT. `src/web/api/routers/work.py:990` reads `submitted_by = body.get('submitted_by')` -- caller-supplied from the POST body, never derived from an authenticated Telegram identity -- and `src/runtime/work_decisions.py:587` defaults it to the literal string 'operator'. `scripts/ops/commit_work_decisions.py:203` then copies that self-asserted string into `answered_by`. POPULATION: the 3 call sites named, read at HEAD 2026-09-03.
items.why_it_matters: The R13 goal was explicitly narrowed from 'a session CANNOT forge this' to 'a session cannot forge this UNDETECTABLY'. As built, neither holds, and the second fails for three independent reasons -- so a guard keyed on this record would read green on a forged approval. (1) `answered_by` is a string the submitter chose; writing 'operator' is free. (2) Git committer name/email are unauthenticated free text: any pusher can set them, so 'committed by the workflow' is not a verifiable property. (3) The obvious hardening -- require the commit to be GitHub-VERIFIED (signed), which a plain `git push` cannot fake -- ALSO fails here, because sessions hold `create_or_update_file` / `push_files`, and commits made through the GitHub API are signed by GitHub and marked verified. Combined with BL-20260903-SESSION-TOKENS-AUTHENTICATE-AS-THE-REPO-OWNER-SO-AN-OWNER-APPROVAL-IS-NOT-AN-IDENTITY-BOUNDARY (sessions authenticate AS `benbaichmankass`), there is NO in-repo signal that separates an operator approval from a session-written one: not the committer, not the signature, not the answered_by string.
items.resolution_criteria: The trustworthy fact must be created where a session cannot reach it: the TELEGRAM BOT knows the real `from_user.id` of whoever tapped the button. Bind `submitted_by` to THAT, server-side, at the bot -- never accept it from the request body -- and record it in the committed row. Then an approval names a Telegram user id that a session cannot manufacture, because it never held the update. Resolution is OBSERVED, not shipped: a real operator tap producing a committed decision row whose `answered_by` is the operator's actual Telegram user id, plus a test proving the route REFUSES a caller-supplied `submitted_by` rather than trusting it. ⚠️ UNTIL THAT EXISTS, R13 MUST NOT CLAIM APPROVAL INDEPENDENCE. Shipping a guard on the current record would be the false independence claim the ruling itself says is worse than the honest current state. ⚠️ AND NOTE THE SCOPE RULING SEPARATELY: the operator narrowed approval to Tier-2/3 only, read from the `tier` field in `.github/pr-landing/<slug>.json`, so the population is already declared -- do not invent a second classification.

items.summary: check_pr_landing.py decides whether a PR is ARMED for auto-merge by one test only -- `_added_or_modified(.github/pr-automerge-requests/<slug>.txt)`. That is the route session PRs use. It is NOT the only route: .github/actions/commit-to-main/action.yml:196 arms GitHub native auto-merge directly with `gh pr merge --auto --squash`, and every machine-generated data PR lands that way. MEASURED 2026-09-03 by reading both files; population: the 2 arming routes in the repo, 1 of which the guard can see.
items.why_it_matters: R10 -- the guard's bite -- fires only when `armed` is true AND the declaration says `landing: hold`. A PR armed through the gh-CLI route reads as NOT armed, so R10 cannot fire on it: such a PR could declare `hold`, be graded `declared_hold`, pass the required check, and then be merged anyway by the auto-merge its own generator enabled. The declaration and reality would disagree in the dangerous direction, silently. This is not currently exploited -- commit-to-main now declares `landing: self`, which is the true statement -- but the guard's blindness is what makes the safe declaration a matter of the author's good faith rather than something checked.
items.resolution_criteria: EITHER the guard learns the second route -- e.g. it treats a diff that adds/modifies a workflow or composite action containing `gh pr merge --auto` as arming, or it reads the PR's `auto_merge` field where the API is available -- with a planted-defect self-test proving a `hold` declaration plus gh-CLI arming FAILS; OR the docstring states the limit explicitly, in the same way it already argues why `.github/pr-automerge-requests/**` is excluded from LANDING_MACHINERY, so a reader knows `armed` means 'armed by the request file' and not 'armed'. ⚠️ NOT resolved by assuming no caller will do this: commit-to-main already does, on every automation PR.

items.summary: MI-98 makes .github/actions/commit-to-main write its own landing declaration (tier 1, landing self), which unlocks the automation PR lane. R5 then grades the diff against check_pr_landing.py's TIER1_SURFACE. MEASURED across all 35 remote automation/* branches, by family: reconcile-open-prs (8), work-digest (4) and strategy-reviews (1) -- the three families currently red-locked -- touch ZERO paths outside the Tier-1 surface, so they pass. But their NEXT run cuts from a current main, writes a `landing: self` declaration, and fails R5 instead of R11. That would trade one lockout for a narrower one, and it would look like a regression introduced by the fix rather than a known gap. Naming it now so the next occurrence is recognised rather than re-diagnosed.

EITHER add `automation/**` and `research/queue/**` to TIER1_SURFACE -- arguable: they are relay bookkeeping and research-queue stamps, no runtime, no config, no order path, and `.github/pr-automerge-requests/**` (which literally arms merges) is already Tier-1 via `.github/**` -- with the argument written into the docstring beside the existing polarity reasoning and a self-test covering the new entries; OR give commit-to-main a per-caller tier/landing input so a family whose paths are not Tier-1 declares something else, and say what that something else is given those PRs DO auto-merge. ⚠️ Widening TIER1_SURFACE widens what can self-land onto main with no human read, which is why this is filed for a decision rather than done. items.title: fetch_standing_wedges turned diag's `present: false` into a synthesised empty ledger, so 12 consecutive digests asserted a clean fleet for a close-wedge ledger the trader had never written
items.summary: The MI-34 downgrade routes broker_cancel_wedged close failures out of the pager and into the work digest. The digest reported 'Standing close wedges: none (ledger read, 0 entries) - a real observation, not an absence of one' on all 12 rows in pending-pings.jsonl, while /api/diag/log_file?name=close_wedge_standing answered present:false at /data/bot-data/runtime_logs/close_wedge_standing.json. The trader had never written the file: sweep_vanished returned before touching disk whenever no wedge was carried, and observe() only writes when recording one. fetch_standing_wedges.unwrap() mapped present:false to EMPTY_LEDGER on the reasoning that a missing file means nothing has ever wedged - an inference not available from a missing file, which is equally consistent with the writer never having run.
items.detail: THE SHAPE, because it is the interesting part: this is the `curl || echo '{}'` collapse the module's OWN docstring warns about, committed in Python inside the function written to prevent it, and shipped with a self-test (case 2) that asserted the defect as correct behaviour ('present:false is an EMPTY READ, not a failure'). Three layers each individually defensible; the defect lived at the seams. NOTE THE FAILURE DIRECTION: this is worse than the 'in neither channel' framing the work order used, because NOT EXAMINED at least sends someone to look, whereas a confident clean bill does not. A latent second defect was found and fixed alongside: work_digest resolved the ledger at REPO_ROOT/runtime_logs/, which agrees with the fetch on a GitHub runner (no DATA_DIR) but diverges anywhere DATA_DIR is set - i.e. on the live VM - the CWD-relative-fallback class canonical-db-resolver forbids for the journal DB, reappearing for a runtime_logs artifact.

items.summary: THE FAILURE: PR #10923 was green and mergeable at 11:01:05Z and merged at 11:11Z. Ten minutes. The OPERATOR noticed before any mechanism did; the manager's own 11:04Z sweep timer trig_016Tn8Kt9sDtQHhxG9NKQabT was `enabled` with `next_run_at: 11:04:00Z` and NEVER FIRED -- no error, no log, no observable state change. WHY THE EXISTING WATCHER CANNOT SEE IT, measured by reading it rather than assumed: `scripts/ops/pr_queue_latency.py` has DEFAULT_THRESHOLD_HOURS = 6.0, and `.github/workflows/pr-queue-watch.yml` runs it on cron `41 */6 * * *`. So the event is below its threshold by a factor of 36 AND below its sampling interval by a factor of 36. Two independent margins, either one sufficient. WORSE, IT MEASURES THE WRONG QUANTITY: `grade_pr` computes `quiet_hours` as hours since the last commit on the head branch, so a PR that JUST went green has quiescence near zero and reads as actively worked -- the exact opposite of 'finished and waiting on the manager'.
items.why_it_matters: The watcher was built 2026-09-02 for the operator directive 'I want actual guards and mechanisms in the repo/vm themselves that watch the manager and enforce the rules on him', and it does catch a real failure -- the ABANDONED PR, 6h+ quiet, which its own measured bimodal distribution (0.2/1.0/1.0 | 5.3/5.7/7.4/7.7/11.0/18.9/109.5) justifies. But 'abandoned' and 'finished and waiting' are different failures with different time constants, and only the first has a watcher. The second is the one that burns sessions: a session at position 1 that has rebased and gone green is BLOCKED on a merge click, and every minute of that is a session idle. ⚠️ AND THE MEASUREMENT THAT MATTERS FOR ANY FIX: check_manager_scope.py's R7 grades the manager's heartbeat cadence, and over 2026-09-03 all 10 same-holder heartbeat gaps were 15-35 minutes (only 1 above 30). The cadence that day was FINE. So a cadence check does NOT cover this and must never be cited as though it did -- that would be a collapsed state.
items.resolution_criteria: A watcher that grades TIME-SINCE-GREEN-AND-MERGEABLE in MINUTES, not hours-since-last-commit, and samples often enough to see it -- a 6-hourly cron cannot observe a 10-minute event at any threshold, so the cadence must change with the metric. Resolution is OBSERVED, not shipped: a real PR going green and the alarm firing before a human notices, with the run recorded. ⚠️ IT MUST NOT LIVE IN PER-PR CI. `check_pr_queue_watch.py` already records why: 'a contributor's PR must never go red because the MANAGER has four other PRs unmerged' -- that punishes the one actor not at fault and trains everyone to ignore the guard. This belongs in the scheduled watcher that already owns the escalation policy. ⚠️ AND THE HARDER HALF, WHICH THIS ROW DOES NOT SOLVE: the 11:04Z sweep was ARMED and silently did not fire, so any fix whose liveness depends on a trigger firing inherits the same hole. Whatever is built must be gradeable from a RECEIPT it writes, the way check_pr_queue_watch.py grades the existing watcher's deadness, rather than from the scheduler's own claim that it is enabled.

items.summary: scripts/ci/run_guards.py computes guard relevance from a COMMIT RANGE, so a run started with uncommitted work silently drops every guard whose relevance depends on the diff. It DOES detect and report this -- 'NOT SELECTED because the work is UNCOMMITTED (17)' -- but it prints that note BELOW the headline summary, and the headline reads `PASS 47 · FAIL 0 · SKIP 38`. MEASURED 2026-09-03 on the MI-102 branch, same tree, back to back: uncommitted run = PASS 47 / FAIL 0 / 17 not selected; committed run = PASS 64 / FAIL 0 / 0 not selected. SEVENTEEN guards did not run, including canonical-doc-coherence, ruff-lint, collapsed-state-guard, new-table-wiring-guard and writer-conformance-guard -- precisely the ones with something to say about the CLAUDE.md edit and the new register file that run was supposed to grade.
items.why_it_matters: `FAIL 0` is the string every reader and every session scans for, and here it is printed about a run the runner ITSELF knows was not a valid grading of the tree. This session nearly reported that 47/0 as a green result and caught it only by reading past the summary. It is the same defect class this repo files under collapsed states -- 'we did not look' rendered identically to 'nothing was wrong' -- and the runner is the single place every guard's verdict is summarised, so a misleading headline there mis-states every guard at once. ⚠️ NOTE THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES IT DANGEROUS: the incomplete run can only ever UNDER-report failures, never over-report them, so it always looks like good news.
items.resolution_criteria: The summary line must not read as a pass when the runner knows the run was incomplete. EITHER the headline carries the count inline (e.g. `PASS 47 · FAIL 0 · SKIP 38 · 17 NOT GRADED (uncommitted)`), OR a run with any not-selected-for-uncommitted guard prints a distinct non-pass state -- the `not_a_pr` / `unattributed` shape this repo already uses for 'nothing was graded here, and that is not a pass'. ⚠️ NOT resolved by exiting non-zero on uncommitted work: local iteration on a dirty tree is the normal way to use this script, and failing it would train people to ignore the runner. The fix is to stop the SUMMARY from claiming more than the run established. Add a self-test asserting the incomplete-run summary is distinguishable from a complete one.

items.summary: Every PR opened through .github/workflows/pr-opener.yml starts with ZERO check runs and stays ungradeable until a human-credentialled actor pushes an extra commit. MEASURED 2026-09-03 on three separate PRs from one session -- #10918, #10923 and #10933 -- each returning `get_check_runs total_count: 0` after the relay opened it, and each needing a hand-made EMPTY commit to become gradeable. POPULATION: 3 of 3 relay-opened PRs this session; 3 of 3 needed the workaround. The cause is documented in pr-opener.yml's own header: the PR is opened by github-actions[bot] under GITHUB_TOKEN, which fires no `pull_request` event, and the bot's own results commit fires no `push` event either.
items.why_it_matters: This is the SAME SHAPE as the draft defect MI-98 fixed hours earlier, and it survived that fix: the relay leaves a PR in a state only a second actor can clear. A PR with zero checks is not merely slow -- auto-merge merges on GREEN, so a PR with no checks waits forever while LOOKING ready, and the spawn template already has to warn sessions about it in prose. Every session that opens a PR through the relay pays the same tax and must know the same folklore, which is the definition of a workflow defect rather than an incident. ⚠️ AND THE WORKAROUND IS ITSELF A HAZARD: the fix is an EMPTY commit, so a session that forgets it has a PR that looks fine and is ungradeable, while a session that remembers pollutes the history with no-op commits -- three of them on main's branches today.
items.resolution_criteria: A PR opened by the relay must arrive gradeable, with no follow-up commit from anyone. Options, to be weighed rather than assumed: open the PR with a PAT rather than GITHUB_TOKEN (the same asymmetry .github/actions/commit-to-main already relies on, whose header states a PAT-opened PR DOES trigger the required checks -- so the precedent exists in this repo and works); OR have the relay itself push the arming commit as its last step, which keeps the no-op commits but removes the folklore; OR give guards.yml a workflow_run trigger so it fires on the relay's own workflow completing. ⚠️ Resolution is OBSERVED: a relay-opened PR showing a non-zero check-run count with no human commit after it. NOT resolved by documenting the workaround better -- the spawn template already documents it, and this session, which had read that documentation, still hit it three times.

items.title: board-post.yml's header says it removes the request file; the code deliberately keeps it, so a session verifying its own post reads the surviving file as a FAILED post
items.detail:
`.github/workflows/board-post.yml`'s docstring (line 22) states the contract as: "writes the resulting comment URL (or the error) to `automation/board-results/<name>.txt`, **removes the request**, and commits the result back". The code does NOT remove it, and that is CORRECT and INTENTIONAL: lines 80-92 record that an earlier version `git rm`'d each request once posted, which made the results commit touch `automation/board-posts/**` -- the workflow's own trigger path -- and the fix was to stop removing it so the results commit stays outside the trigger. So the header is stale prose describing a behaviour that was deliberately removed, sitting nine lines above the comment block explaining why it was removed. FIELD BEATS COMMENT; the header is the half that is wrong.

WHY IT IS WORTH A ROW rather than a silent one-line edit: the stale sentence produces a FALSE NEGATIVE on the exact check a session performs to verify its own board post. board-post.yml is reached only when `add_issue_comment` 403s, i.e. by a session that cannot read the board back through the MCP write path and must verify from the branch instead. Following the documented contract, that session tests `does the request file still exist?` and reads STILL PRESENT as `the post did not complete`. Measured this session on 2026-09-03: the request file survived, the result file held a bare comment URL (`#issuecomment-5523621097`), and the run exited 0 -- a SUCCESSFUL post that the documented check grades as a failure. The correct discriminators are already in the code and are not in the header: the failure path writes `FAILED:\n<url>` to the result file (line 114) and the run exits 1 (line 152).

This is UNPROVENANCED DIAGNOSTIC OUTPUT sub-class A as CLAUDE.md defines it -- a stated contract naming a condition (`request file removed`) that no code path produces -- and it lands on a relay whose whole design premise is that a failed post must be LOUD, because "a session that believes it claimed the board and did not is invisible to every other session AND to itself". The stale header inverts that in the other direction: a session that DID claim the board concludes it did not, and either re-posts (duplicating on #6927) or reports its own board post as failed.

REMEDY: correct the header to state what the code does -- the request file is deliberately left in place, and success/failure is read from the RESULT file's `FAILED:` prefix and the run's exit status, never from the request file's presence. Keep the lines 80-92 rationale; it is the reason the behaviour is right. Population note: n=1 session misled, caught within one tool call because the workflow body was read rather than trusted -- the cost is bounded, the direction is not.
items.resolution_criteria: The header no longer contains the sentence "removes the request", and states instead that the request file is deliberately left in place and that success is read from the RESULT file (a bare comment URL, run exit 0) versus failure (a `FAILED:` prefix, run exit 1). Verified by two commands rather than by reading the prose: `grep -c 'removes the request' .github/workflows/board-post.yml` returns 0, and `grep -c 'FAILED:' .github/workflows/board-post.yml` returns a non-zero count inside the header block. NOT sufficient: the workflow continuing to work -- it already works, and the defect is in what it TELLS a session about itself. NOT sufficient either: this row being filed. The observable that would reopen it is a later session again reporting a successful board post as failed, or re-posting a duplicate on #6927, on the strength of the request file's presence.

items.title: pr-opener.yml reads the draft flag with `jq '.draft // true'`, and jq's // treats false as absent — so `"draft": false` is UNREACHABLE, every relay-opened PR is a draft, and the Tier-1 self-landing route MI-88 shipped cannot be satisfied by the 403'd sessions it exists for
items.title_short: pr-opener: `draft: false` unreachable, Tier-1 cannot self-land
items.detail:
MEASURED 2026-09-03 on PR #10920. The request file `automation/pr-requests/mi92-board-post-header-drift-20260903a.json` contained `"draft": false` (verified: `jq -r '.draft' <file>` -> `false`). The PR opened `draft: true`.

CAUSE, at `.github/workflows/pr-opener.yml` line 123:
    [ "$(jq -r '.draft // true' "$req")" = "true" ] && draft_flag="--draft"
jq's `//` is the ALTERNATIVE operator, not a null-coalesce: it falls through when the left side is `null` OR `false`. So the expression returns `true` for all three inputs, verified directly:
    .draft=false -> true | .draft=null -> true | .draft=true -> true
`"draft": false` therefore cannot be expressed. EVERY PR this relay opens is a draft, regardless of what the request asks for. The correct form is `if .draft == null then true else .draft end` (or `.draft // true` replaced by an explicit `has("draft")` test) — keeping `true` as the DEFAULT, which is right, while making `false` REACHABLE, which it is not today.

WHY THIS IS STRUCTURAL AND NOT COSMETIC. `.github/pr-landing/README.md` states that Tier-1 self-landing needs BOTH halves and that neither alone suffices: `"draft": false` decides READINESS, and `.github/pr-automerge-requests/<slug>.txt` decides LANDING. `claude-pr-automerge.yml` line 219 then REFUSES to un-draft a PR it did not itself open — correctly, by design, since a draft is this repo's marker for 'prepared, not approved'. Compose the three and the readiness half is unreachable through the relay: a session whose MCP `create_pull_request` 403s — THE EXACT POPULATION THE RELAY EXISTS FOR — can satisfy every instruction the landing route gives and still produce a draft that auto-merge refuses. Tier-1 self-landing is, for that session, IMPOSSIBLE. That is the same observable state MI-88 was dispatched to fix (a green Tier-1 PR nobody merges), reproduced inside the mechanism built to fix it. The README's own refusal message even instructs the reader to 'open it non-draft (request file `"draft": false`)', which is the one thing that cannot work.

IT ALSO CONTRADICTS A WRITTEN ACCUSATION AGAINST PRIOR SESSIONS, and that half matters independently. `.github/pr-landing/README.md` lines 19-23 say: "Three of those PR bodies blamed `pr-opener.yml` for 'creating every PR as a draft regardless of `draft:false`'. THAT IS FALSE AND SHOULD NOT BE REPEATED. `pr-opener.yml` honours `draft:false`; `true` is only the default, and those sessions' request files asked for `"draft": true`." The code says the three sessions described the behaviour CORRECTLY. Whatever those particular request files contained, the general claim they made is true and the README's correction is not — so the README is currently instructing every future session to dismiss an accurate bug report. Field beats comment.

RELATIONSHIP TO BL-20260903-A-PR-OPENED-BY-THE-RELAY-CAN-ARM-AUTOMERGE-AND-THEN-WAIT-ON-GREEN-FOREVER (open): NOT a duplicate, and it EXPLAINS that row's loose end. That row is about zero-checks-plus-auto-merge stalling, and records of MI-88's own PR #10894 that 'that PR was a DRAFT and so had not armed auto-merge, meaning the STALL ITSELF is still inferred from (a)+(b) rather than sighted'. The draft there is treated as incidental. It is not incidental — it is FORCED, by this bug, on every PR the relay opens including #10894 and #10920. Fixing this one is what would let the other be observed rather than inferred; the two should be read together and this one is upstream.

SEPARATELY CONFIRMED SAME DAY: #10920 also came back `mergeable_state: blocked` with `total_count: 0`, the zero-checks half, because the relay's own results commit is authored by `github-actions[bot]` and GITHUB_TOKEN pushes trigger no workflows. Both halves of the trap fired on one PR.
items.resolution_criteria: A PR opened THROUGH pr-opener.yml from a request file containing `"draft": false` comes back `draft: false` on `pull_request_read` — read the PR's own draft field, never the workflow diff and never the request file. NOT sufficient: the jq expression being changed (that is the fix, not the observation); a unit test of the expression; or a PR opened by `create_pull_request` via the MCP, which never had this bug and would prove nothing. The default must be verified UNCHANGED in the same pass: a request file that OMITS `draft` entirely must still produce `draft: true`, since `true` is the correct default and a fix that inverts it would arm auto-merge on every Tier-2/3 PR the relay opens. Additionally, `.github/pr-landing/README.md` lines 19-23 no longer assert that sessions reporting this behaviour are wrong.
items.tier: 1 — a one-expression fix in a .github workflow plus a README correction; no runtime, order path, strategy config or risk cap. NOTE it is landing machinery, so pr-landing-guard R12 will require `landing: "hold"` and one human read before it merges.

items.title: The standing close-wedge ledger does not exist, and the digest that replaced the pager reads a non-canonical path for it
items.summary: MEASURED 2026-09-03 via /api/diag/log_file?name=close_wedge_standing: `{"path": "/data/bot-data/runtime_logs/close_wedge_standing.json", "present": false, "lines": []}`. TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS, and they must not be collapsed. (1) THE DIGEST READS THE WRONG PATH. The 2026-09-03 work digest reported the ledger absent at `/home/ubuntu/ict-trading-bot/runtime_logs/close_wedge_standing.json`, while diag resolves it under `$DATA_DIR` at `/data/bot-data/runtime_logs/`. That is the CWD-relative-fallback class `canonical-db-resolver` exists to forbid for the journal DB, reappearing for a runtime_logs artifact -- so even once the writer works, the digest would keep reporting NOT EXAMINED. (2) THE LEDGER IS ABSENT AT THE CANONICAL PATH TOO, so the writer has never written it. ⚠️ WHY THIS IS NOT COSMETIC: on 2026-09-02 (MI-34) the operator DELIBERATELY DOWNGRADED close failures whose share_hold reads `broker_cancel_wedged` OUT of the paging channel and INTO this digest, on the reasoning that a wedge no bot-side lever can clear should not page repeatedly. That downgrade is only safe if the digest channel actually carries them. With no ledger and a mis-pathed reader, such a failure is currently in NEITHER CHANNEL -- the digest says so in its own words: 'an un-fetched ledger means such an item is currently in NEITHER channel'. This is an observability hole on a real-money close path.
items.evidence: /api/diag/log_file?name=close_wedge_standing returned present:false for /data/bot-data/runtime_logs/close_wedge_standing.json, read 2026-09-03 from the manager session via the Caddy direct path (served by https://ict-bot.duckdns.org). The 2026-09-03 work digest text names /home/ubuntu/ict-trading-bot/runtime_logs/close_wedge_standing.json as the path it checked.
items.resolution_criteria: BOTH halves, and say which you cleared. (a) The digest and any other reader resolve this artifact through the canonical $DATA_DIR-based resolver rather than a repo-relative path -- verified by the digest naming /data/bot-data/... in its own output, not by reading the code. (b) The absence is DISAMBIGUATED. `present: false` today cannot distinguish 'no wedge has occurred since the writer shipped' from 'the writer is not running', and those are opposite facts -- the collapsed-state failure this repo files bugs about. The writer must emit an empty-but-present ledger with a timestamp so that `wedges: []` means WE LOOKED AND FOUND NONE, distinct from a missing file meaning WE DID NOT LOOK. ⚠️ NOT SUFFICIENT: creating the file by hand; the writer must produce it. ⚠️ AND CHECK THE DOWNGRADE IS STILL SAFE: while (b) is unresolved, confirm whether any broker_cancel_wedged close failure has occurred since MI-34 shipped -- if one has, it was silently in neither channel and that is an incident, not a gap.
items.notes: Surfaced because the operator pasted the digest into the manager session; the digest's own NOT EXAMINED warning is what prompted the read. The warning text is well-written and did its job -- it is the reader path and the writer that are wrong, not the alarm.

items.title: The manager lease heartbeat lands on the manager's BRANCH, so origin/main lags it by however long that PR takes to merge
items.summary: MEASURED 2026-09-03T09:50Z from the live manager session: `docs/claude/work/MANAGER-LEASE.json` on origin/main carries `heartbeat_at: 2026-09-03T09:21:42Z` while the manager's working tree carries `09:48:17Z` — a 27-minute lag, because `manager_lease.py heartbeat` writes the file into the manager's own branch and it only reaches `main` when that branch's PR merges. ⚠️ CLAUDE.md's own lease contract says 'A claim you did not PUSH protects nothing — another session reads origin, not your working tree.' That warning is about PUSHING, and it is insufficient: the manager HAD pushed, on every heartbeat, and origin/main was still 27 minutes stale. The gap is branch-vs-main, not pushed-vs-unpushed, and the documented warning does not describe it. ⚠️ WHY IT IS NOT MERELY UNTIDY: takeover is TIME-BASED on a 90-minute TTL precisely so that a manager which DIED cannot block its successor. A lag consumes the safety margin — a 27-minute lag spends 30% of it -- 27 of 90 minutes, arithmetic on the two figures measured above, POPULATION n=1: the single 09:50Z read of origin/main's MANAGER-LEASE.json against the manager's working tree. One observation, not a distribution -- the lag's distribution is unmeasured and is bounded by nothing except how long the manager's PR takes to merge — and the lag is bounded by nothing except how long the manager's PR takes to merge. TODAY THAT WAS NOT HYPOTHETICAL: two PRs sat conflicted for over an hour this morning, and the manager's own branch has been conflicted before. If a manager's PR were blocked for 90+ minutes while the manager was ALIVE and heartbeating every 20 minutes, a cold successor reading origin/main would grade the lease EXPIRED and claim it — producing exactly the two-concurrent-managers state the operator's 'exactly one management session at a time' requirement exists to forbid, with both sessions believing they hold it.
items.evidence: git show origin/main:docs/claude/work/MANAGER-LEASE.json -> heartbeat_at 2026-09-03T09:21:42Z; working tree of session_01Nopk1HcpvWBSEbZxEmALkd on claude/workflow-overhaul-scope-z4sjm3 -> 09:48:17Z. Read 2026-09-03T09:50Z. The 09:21:42Z value reached main via PR #10917, which merged at ~09:31Z.
items.resolution_criteria: The lease's freshness on origin/main is bounded by the heartbeat cadence rather than by a PR's merge latency. Candidates, not yet chosen: (a) heartbeat commits directly to main through the existing commit-to-main action, the way other receipts do — the lease is a receipt, not reviewable content, so a PR adds nothing; (b) the reader treats a lease found on a live manager BRANCH as authoritative, which is more complex and re-introduces 'which branch do I trust'; (c) the TTL is widened, which is the wrong direction — it makes a genuinely dead manager block its successor for longer. ⚠️ VERIFY BY MEASUREMENT, NOT BY CODE READING: after the fix, compare origin/main's heartbeat_at against the manager's own clock across at least three heartbeats and state the max lag. ⚠️ AND CHECK THE HISTORICAL QUESTION SEPARATELY: has any takeover ever occurred against a lease whose origin/main copy was stale while its holder was alive? MANAGER-LEASE.json's git history (59 revisions across 3 sessions as of 2026-09-03) is where that is answerable, and a `--force` claim carrying a reason is where it would show.
items.notes: Found because a stop hook flagged the uncommitted heartbeat, which prompted comparing the two copies. The manager had been heartbeating and pushing correctly throughout — the defect is structural, not a missed step.

items.title: The manager's whole supervision cadence rode one send_later timer with no delivery guarantee and no detector, and it silently did not fire
items.summary: MEASURED 2026-09-03T11:13Z. Trigger `trig_016Tn8Kt9sDtQHhxG9NKQabT` ("Manager sweep (5-min cadence)") was created 10:58:41Z with `run_once_at` / `next_run_at` = 11:04:00Z. At 11:13Z `list_triggers` still showed it `enabled: true` with `next_run_at` in the PAST and no delivery -- it never fired and never errored. CONSEQUENCE, measured not inferred: PR #10923's last check (`pytest-run`) completed SUCCESS at 11:01:05Z, making it fully green and mergeable; it was merged at 11:11Z, and the thing that surfaced it was THE OPERATOR ASKING, not the mechanism. ~10 minutes of a green position-1 PR sitting unmerged, and ~13 minutes of total manager silence, during a period when the operator had explicitly said a manager idle for 30 minutes 'should basically never happen'. ⚠️ THE DEFECT IS NOT THAT A TIMER MISSED -- it is that the manager's ENTIRE supervision cadence was a SINGLE unmonitored timer. There was no second carrier and, worse, NO DETECTOR: a `send_later` that does not deliver produces no error, no log the session sees, and no state change the session can notice -- the session simply never wakes. That is indistinguishable from a manager that decided to do nothing, which is exactly the collapse this repo keeps filing: 'we did not look' and 'there was nothing to do' rendering identically. ⚠️ AND THE REPO ALREADY KNEW THIS CLASS: `OI-20260902-DIGEST-MOVED-OFF-A-CRON-THAT-DOES-NOT-FIRE` records GitHub cron firing 5 times against 24 declared, and `work_digest_now.py`'s own docstring says outright that 'GitHub Actions cron is not a clock in this repo'. The same lesson had not been applied to the manager's own wake mechanism.

Interim mitigation already applied: two overlapping send_later wakeups (~4 min and ~7 min) so one miss does not open a gap -- that is redundancy, NOT a detector, and must not be reported as a fix. ⚠️ THE DETECTOR IS THE HARDER AND MORE IMPORTANT HALF: the gap must be measured from the OUTSIDE, against what the manager actually DID, never against what it scheduled. `MANAGER-LEASE.json`'s git history is the natural instrument because it records heartbeats that HAPPENED (59 revisions across 3 sessions as of 2026-09-03; gaps median 18 min, p90 66, max 480). items.title: 25 of 26 landed_unproven rows name no monitoring carrier, so a row that IS being watched and a row nobody is watching render identically
items.summary: OPERATOR DIRECTIVE 2026-09-03, verbatim: 'if there are items for which we can't manufacture a reliable test, then we need to log them to be monitored so that once they get triggered in real life, we can observe and verify or fix.' MEASURED IMMEDIATELY AFTER, and the mechanism the directive asks for ALREADY EXISTS AND IS POPULATED -- docs/claude/OPEN-ITEMS.json holds 51 rows of which 34 are `kind: monitoring`, and spot-checking the six hardest-to-test items (the Phase F/D/G/H rows and the two role-pack rows) found a plausible monitoring row for EVERY ONE. So the gap is NOT missing monitoring. THE GAP IS THE LINKAGE, AND IT IS ONE-DIRECTIONAL: of the 26 rows sitting at `landed_unproven` in MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json, exactly **1 names an OI- monitoring row (3%)**, while 11 of the 51 OPEN-ITEMS rows name an MI- checklist row. The monitoring register knows what it is watching; the work register does not know it is being watched. CONSEQUENCE: a manager reading the checklist sees '26 unproven' and CANNOT DISTINGUISH a row that is CARRIED -- something is watching it and it will clear when the condition triggers in real life -- from a row that is ORPHANED, where nobody is watching and it will sit at landed_unproven forever. Those are opposite facts rendering identically, which is the collapsed-state failure this repo files bugs about, occurring in the register that exists to prevent exactly that.
items.evidence: Measured 2026-09-03T11:52Z over docs/claude/work/MANAGER-CHECKLIST.json (97 items, 26 at landed_unproven) and docs/claude/OPEN-ITEMS.json (51 items, 34 monitoring). Substring scan for 'OI-2026' across each landed_unproven row: 1 of 26. Substring scan for 'MI-<digit>' across each OPEN-ITEMS row: 11 of 51.
items.resolution_criteria: A `landed_unproven` row must NAME its carrier or explicitly declare it has none. Concretely: (a) a `monitored_by` field naming the OI- row that will clear it, OR an explicit `monitored_by: null` WITH a reason -- and `null` must be a deliberate, readable state, never an absent field, because an absent field is precisely what makes carried and orphaned identical today; (b) a CHECK that fails when a row sits at `landed_unproven` with neither. ⚠️ THE CHECK IS THE POINT, NOT THE ONE-OFF LINKING PASS: the operator's standing rule is that these become hard mechanisms rather than habits, and a manual pass restores the same gap the next time a row lands. ⚠️ AND DO NOT INVENT A CARRIER TO SATISFY THE FIELD -- pointing a row at a monitoring row that does not actually cover it is worse than the honest null, because it converts 'nobody is watching' into a false claim that someone is. Where no monitoring row genuinely covers a landed_unproven row, the correct action is to FILE one with an honest clears_when, which is what the operator asked for.
items.notes: Found while acting on the operator's directive rather than by audit. The directive assumed the monitoring did not exist; the measurement shows it does, and that what is missing is the join. Filing the true finding rather than the one that was asked about.

items.title: health-review-backlog.json runs THREE different creation-date key names, backlog_append.py enforces none, and check_register_ids accepts only one — so every session filing a row lands red with no warning
items.detail: MEASURED 2026-09-03, three separate sessions inside four hours. scripts/ci/check_register_ids.py landed on main at 10:08:56Z (#10910) and requires a NEW backlog row to carry one of ['opened_at','opened']. The register in fact carries at least THREE names for that one fact: 'found_on' (the two rows MI-92's session filed on #10920), 'filed' (the four rows the manager filed at ~11:25Z), and 'opened_at' (what the guard accepts). scripts/ops/backlog_append.py — the sanctioned, mandatory appender, which CLAUDE.md says to use and never hand-edit — writes whatever dict the caller hands it and enforces NO creation-date key at all. So the mandated tool produces rows the mandated guard rejects. OBSERVED CONSEQUENCE, not hypothetical: #10920 was 8/8 green at 12:04Z; merging main in pulled the guard forward and turned it red on two rows that were correct when written, and the manager branch went red on four of its own. POPULATION: 6 rows across 2 branches and 3 sessions, all filed 2026-09-03, all rejected for the same reason. The guard is RIGHT that a creation fact is needed — its reasoning is sound (to git a reused id is a changed value at one key, so a merge silently deletes the row already there). The defect is that nothing tells a session which key to use, and the one tool they are required to use does not supply it.
items.evidence: check_register_ids.py --base origin/main on both branches; key lists read directly off the rows: ['id','title','detail','resolution_criteria','severity','tier','status','area','found_by','found_on'] vs ['id','title','severity','status','tier','filed','area','summary','evidence','resolution_criteria','notes'] vs the exemplar ['id','opened_at','opened_by',...]. grep for opened_at/filed in scripts/ops/backlog_append.py returns nothing.
items.resolution_criteria: backlog_append.py STAMPS a creation date under the key the guard accepts when the caller omits one, so the sanctioned path cannot produce a rejected row — and it is proven by a test that appends a row with no date and asserts check_register_ids passes on the result. NOT SUFFICIENT: documenting the key name, which is the reminder-instead-of-mechanism non-fix this repo has already paid for. The pre-existing 'found_on'/'filed' rows should be left alone rather than swept: they are only graded when they are NEW in a diff, and rewriting thousands of rows to normalise a key would re-attribute the whole file.
items.notes: Do NOT resolve this by relaxing the guard to accept found_on/filed. That widens the accepted set without making the appender produce anything, so the next session inventing a fourth name fails the same way.

items.title: check_register_ids.py prints `register-id-guard: OK` and exits 0 on a register that is UNPARSEABLE JSON — 'we could not look' collapses into 'we looked and found nothing', in the guard whose whole job is register integrity
items.detail: FOUND BY ACCIDENT 2026-09-03, then CONFIRMED DELIBERATELY. A textual edit to docs/claude/health-review-backlog.json left a missing comma (the key being appended after was last in its object). json.load raised JSONDecodeError at line 31741 while, on the very same file, `python3 scripts/ci/check_register_ids.py --base origin/main` printed 'docs/claude/health-review-backlog.json::items[id]: not present or not parseable — not checked' and then 'register-id-guard: OK', exit 0. Reproduced on purpose afterwards by inserting the literal text 'THIS IS NOT JSON' after the items array opener: same output, same exit 0. So a corrupted register — the single failure mode most likely to DESTROY rows, which is exactly what this guard exists to prevent — reads to CI as a clean pass. The line 'not present or not parseable — not checked' is honest and is printed; the VERDICT built on top of it is not, and a reader sees the verdict. Note the two states it merges are themselves different facts: a register that does not exist yet and a register that has been corrupted are opposite conditions and should not share a message either. STATE THE POPULATION: observed on health-review-backlog.json only; the same helper drives all 10 declared register arrays, so the behaviour is presumed shared but was measured on one. NOT UNBOUNDED: pytest-collect and other consumers would likely fail on broken JSON elsewhere in the same CI run, so a corrupt register is unlikely to reach main silently — but that is other guards covering for this one, not this one working.
items.evidence: Two runs on /tmp/wt10920 at ~13:1xZ: (1) accidental — json.decoder.JSONDecodeError line 31741 col 7 alongside 'register-id-guard: OK'; (2) deliberate — items array opener corrupted, guard prints the same OK and exits 0. Restored and re-verified parseable both times.
items.resolution_criteria: A register that is present but does NOT parse makes the guard FAIL, loudly, naming the file and the parse error — and 'absent' stays a separate, distinguishable state from 'unparseable', because a register that has never existed and one that was just corrupted call for opposite actions. Proven by a planted-defect case in the guard's own --self-test: a corrupted register must fail, an absent one must report absent, and a clean tree must still pass as the positive control.
items.notes: This is the `collapsed-state` doctrine applied to a guard's own verdict rather than to a data field. Registering a contract in check_collapsed_states.py's CONTRACTS table may be the right shape, since the three states (parsed / absent / unparseable) are exactly the shape that guard grades.
